When execution happens elsewhere, developers must move code into a notebook, run it, and bring the results or errors back to the agent. FNTK connects those steps so the agent can work with a running Fabric notebook and its execution results instead of relying only on code shared in the conversation.

Interactive development and debugging are the central use cases. You can ask an agent to inspect a notebook, investigate a failing transformation, or validate a change using actual execution output. The notebook remains in Fabric and uses Fabric capacity for distributed data processing, while FNTK provides the terminal commands the agent uses to interact with the live session.

Run, inspect, and refine one cell at a time

FNTK keeps the notebook session active while the agent works, so developers can explore and refine code without repeatedly restarting the workflow. For example, an agent can inspect a schema, adjust a conversion, check several records, and return to the same transformation as new information emerges. This mirrors the iterative way developers work in notebooks and keeps each change grounded in actual execution results.

The toolkit brings the operations needed for that workflow into the terminal. An agent can discover the target notebook, read and update its cells, execute code, and retrieve results. Instead of treating every adjustment as a new whole-notebook submission, it can focus on the code being investigated.

  • Find workspaces, notebooks, and lakehouses to establish the context for the task.
  • Read, add, or update notebook cells as the work develops.
  • Execute a cell's code and inspect its output before deciding what to change.
  • Reuse the live session to refine and rerun the relevant code.

For example, a transformation may fail because an input column has a different type than expected. An agent can inspect the schema, revise the affected code, and rerun it in the existing session to check the result. This avoids restarting the entire notebook merely to test that change and keeps the investigation focused on the failing operation.

Give the agent the evidence to debug

FNTK gives the agent the execution evidence needed to determine the source of a failure. It exposes cell output and Spark job state, along with driver logs, executor logs, and logs from Livy, the service that manages Spark sessions. With this context, the agent can investigate the likely source of a problem instead of relying on source code alone.

The CLI can return structured JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) responses that identify results, errors, and suggested next actions. An agent can use this information to determine whether execution has finished, retrieve diagnostics, and choose what to investigate next. This shortens the feedback loop between writing code and understanding its behavior while reducing the need to copy outputs and logs manually between tools.

FNTK in practice at Microsoft

For our data engineering team at Microsoft, FNTK filled a gap between generating code and working with real data. Previously, we used an AI assistant to draft code locally, then copied it into Fabric notebooks to run it and brought the results back into the conversation. With FNTK, we can stay in GitHub Copilot, execute code in Fabric, and use the results to iterate.

We started by installing the toolkit, connecting with the appropriate permissions, and asking questions about a data source. Exploratory work quickly became a valuable use case. We could ask for row counts, distributions, or samples, then follow up based on the actual results. From there, we built shared workflow skills and a developer plugin around FNTK, incorporated our engineering standards, and connected the plugin to Azure DevOps through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to bring user-story context into the same workflow.

In practice, this has sped up development and helped us work across multiple user stories, with more of our time spent reviewing changes rather than writing every line ourselves. Copilot handles the reasoning; FNTK provides the connection to live notebook execution. We can still inspect the runs in Fabric, and our existing source-control, quality, and human-review practices remain in place.

In practice, this workflow has helped us work across multiple user stories and spend more time reviewing changes instead of writing every line ourselves. Copilot handles the reasoning; FNTK provides the connection to live notebook execution. We can still inspect the runs in Fabric, and our existing source-control, quality, and human-review practices remain in place.

Figure: FNTK connects an AI developer agent to live Fabric notebook execution, alongside MCP tools for context and delivery tools for human-reviewed changes.

Capabilities with FNTK commands

Command or group

Usage

fntk help

Show command guidance and examples.

fntk init

Install or update coding agent workflow skills.

fntk discover

Find workspaces, notebooks, lakehouses, and identity information.

fntk notebook

Manage notebooks, sessions, and default lakehouses.

fntk cell

Read, edit, and organize notebook cells.

fntk code

Execute code, retrieve results, and cancel runs.

fntk monitor

Inspect Spark progress, diagnostics, and resource usage.

fntk logs

Download driver, executor, Livy, and cell logs.

fntk resource

Manage notebook resource files and folders.

fntk skill

Read built-in coding and debugging guidance.

fntk server

Manage the local FNTK server.

Get started

To try the workflow, install the toolkit and connect your coding agent by following the FNTK installation and quick-start documentation, including fntk init for workflow skill setup. Then choose an existing development notebook and a focused task, such as inspecting one transformation. Run the code, review the output, and use the result to guide your next change.

fabric_blog:5c86ce454fa4.title: From mixed events to real-time action: Fabric Eventstreams Q3 2026
fabric_blog:5c86ce454fa4.excerpt:
Coauthor: Arindam Chatterjee

Fabric Eventstreams makes it easy to connect to streaming sources, transform the ingested events and route them to destinations across Microsoft Fabric. But building real-time systems also requires teams to understand the events in motion, enriching them with business context, detecting and responding to any issues on time, and securely managing their streams across environments.

That broader experience is the story behind this quarter’s updates. Eventstreams is expanding beyond connectivity and data movement to provide more of the capabilities teams need to work with streaming data after it arrives, while it is still in motion.

With these expanded capabilities, users can now:

  • Connect to more managed sources and extend Eventstreams with custom connectors.
  • Capture change feeds from more operational databases.
  • Explore and process multiple event types in a single Eventstream.
  • Enrich streaming events with contextual data before processing and routing.
  • Monitor processing health, diagnose problems, and act faster.
  • Deploy with workspace-scoped networking and reusable configuration.

Connect managed and custom streaming sources

Eventstream added generally available managed connectors for SAP Datasphere, Cribl, Solace PubSub+, and MQTT, extending native connectivity across enterprise applications, observability pipelines, event meshes, and IoT brokers. For these common scenarios, teams can use managed connectors instead of writing and hosting connector code. 

Managed connectors cover a growing range of common sources. But many organizations also need to connect proprietary applications, partner products, and internal platforms. 

Custom Stream Connector (Preview) lets organizations bring compatible Kafka Connect source connectors into Fabric when a native connector is unavailable. Teams can manage versions, publish connectors internally or through a partner, and make them discoverable in Real-Time hub. This approach extends managed Fabric pipelines to proprietary applications, partner products, and internal platforms while allowing independent software vendors to retain control of their code and licensing. 

What shipped: SAP Datasphere connector (Generally Available), Cribl connector (Generally Available), Solace PubSub+ connector (Generally Available), MQTT connector (Generally Available), Custom Stream Connector (Preview).

Bring operational changes into the stream

Orders, inventory updates, account changes, and application state already live in operational databases. Capturing those changes is only the first step. Teams must also operate connectors, recover from failures, handle schema changes, and scale the pipeline. This complex operational work makes many CDC-based solutions difficult to sustain. 

Two connectors reaching general availability this quarter move more of that burden into Eventstream. The Mirrored Database Change Feed connector consumes row-level inserts, updates, and deletes from change-feed-enabled mirrored databases. The MongoDB CDC connector supports MongoDB Atlas, cloud-hosted, and self-managed deployments. Both bring database changes into Eventstream's managed processing model, ready for the same DeltaFlow transformations available to other CDC sources. 

What shipped: Mirrored Database Change Feed connector (Generally Available), MongoDB CDC connector (Generally Available)

Understand every event shape

Streaming data rarely arrives in one consistent shape. A source may carry messages from multiple device types, application payloads may evolve, and teams may combine sources to improve utilization and reduce cost. Treating every payload as a union of every possible field makes exploration harder and creates long fragile transformations. 

Schema Registry and Event Schema Sets (Generally Available) provide reusable contracts for streaming data. Teams can define Avro schemas, group related schemas, retain earlier versions, compare changes, and discover schemas across Fabric workspaces. 

Schema-aware Eventstreams (Preview) lets one eventstream understand and process multiple event types. Events with registered schemas, along with change feeds from supported operational databases, are recognized automatically. For unschematized payloads, users can classify events with a field such as deviceType or entityType.

A redesigned data preview makes it easier to inspect each event: 

  • Browse and inspect nested JSON structures
  • View event headers and metadata along with the actual payload
  • Download selected events
Figure: Processing mixed events from schematized and un-schematized sources within a single schema-aware eventstream

What shipped: Schema Registry and Event Schema Sets (Generally Available), Schema-aware Eventstreams (Preview).

Add business context in flight

Live events often contain only a device ID, customer ID, or product code. Without the surrounding business context, downstream systems cannot make an informed decision until a separate batch process enriches the data once it reaches an analytical store.

Reference Data with Delta Table (Preview) brings that enrichment into Eventstream. A live event can join with reference data in a Lakehouse or warehouse table, including shortcut-backed Delta tables. No-code INNER and LEFT OUTER joins cover common patterns, while the SQL experience supports more complex logic. The event gains business meaning before it is routed, not after. 

Figure: Reference Data Join adds business context to an event before it's routed to a destination.

What shipped: Reference Data with Delta table (Preview)

Detect issues and act faster

A streaming pipeline can appear to be running even when a node falls behind, events arrive outside the expected time window, or a destination rejects processed values. A top-level running state is not enough to diagnose these conditions.

This quarter adds a more complete operating loop around each Eventstream. Workspace Monitoring helps teams observe throughput, backlog, watermark delay, errors, and node health. Processing logs and editor validation help diagnose malformed input, query failures, type-conversion errors, event-time policy violations, recovery events, and destination-access problems. Teams can act by creating and managing Activator rules without leaving Eventstream, then optimize capacity by routing Capacity Operation Events through Eventstream for operation-level analysis, alerting, and governance.

What shipped: Workspace Monitoring for Eventstream (Preview), Workspace Monitoring diagnostic-log support (Preview), Activator rule management in Eventstream (Generally Available), Capacity Operation Events source (Preview).

Secure and deploy eventstreams consistently

Enterprise streaming workloads often need private connectivity, environment-specific configuration, and explicit control over where data can flow.

Workspace-level Private Link (Preview) for Eventstream lets administrators apply private inbound connectivity to selected Fabric workspaces instead of imposing the same network posture across the tenant.

Variable Library support (Preview) keeps environment-specific connections, item references, parameters, and value sets separate from pipeline logic. Teams can carry one Eventstream across development, test, and production without embedding each environment's values in the definition. These capabilities build on existing support for private and on-premises sources, workspace identity, custom certificate authorities, mutual TLS, and outbound access protection.

What shipped: Workspace-level Private Link for Eventstream (Preview), Variable Library support for Eventstream (Preview).

What this quarter adds up to

Together, these updates create a more complete path from incoming events to business action. Teams can understand mixed payloads, enrich events while they are moving, bring in operational changes, connect managed or custom sources, diagnose processing problems, and carry the same Eventstream safely across environments. 

This quarter also brings an early glimpse of how Eventstreams can connect streaming and batch data movement more closely. Copy Job support for Eventstreams (Preview) enables an Eventstream to be used as either a source or destination in the Copy Job experience, creating an initial bridge between the two. The experience starts in Copy Job today, but it points toward more connected data movement experiences across Fabric.

Fabric Eventstreams is expanding beyond ingestion to help teams shape, enrich, monitor, and govern real-time data as it moves from source to business action.

Resources

Generally Available

  • Schema Registry in Fabric Real-Time Intelligence
  • Add Mirrored Database Change Feed source to an eventstream
  • Add MongoDB CDC source to an eventstream
  • Add an SAP Datasphere source to an eventstream
  • Add Cribl source to an eventstream
  • Add Solace PubSub+ as source to an eventstream
  • MQTT Source in Fabric Eventstream
  • Add a Fabric Activator Destination to an Eventstream

Preview

  • Schema-Aware Eventstreams Overview (Preview)
  • Enrich Events with Reference Data in Fabric Eventstreams
  • Add a custom stream connector to an eventstream
  • Eventstream Workspace Monitoring Overview (preview)
  • Fabric Capacity Operation Source in Fabric Eventstream
  • Secure inbound connections with Tenant and Workspace Private Links
  • Variable Library Integration with Eventstreams

For the full release roundup, including items outside this post's scope, see the August 2026 Fabric Feature Summary and the September 2026 Fabric Feature Summary.

Get started

Start with the capability above that most closely matches what your team needs, then follow its documentation links to try the corresponding Eventstream feature(s) in your workspace. Found a gap, a bug, or a scenario these features do not cover? Share it through Fabric Ideas or directly with us on the Eventstream PM team. Your feedback helps shape what comes next.

fabric_blog:07b39f8f1c18.title: More expressive graph analysis: GQL improvements in Microsoft Fabric Graph
fabric_blog:07b39f8f1c18.excerpt:
Coauthors: Idris Motiwala, and Justin Fine

January–August 2026 updates expand how users find, inspect, compose, and analyze connections.

Organizations use graph data to understand how information moves between systems, how services depend on one another, how conversations develop, and how people or organizations relate. Graph Query Language (GQL) in Microsoft Fabric Graph helps users explore and analyze those connections with standardized query patterns. 

From January through August 2026, new GQL capabilities made it easier to control traversals, inspect paths, compose multistage queries, summarize connected data, and work with complex values. These improvements help analysts express more graph questions in a single query and give developers finer control over query behavior. The following sections explain where each capability is useful and show the associated syntax. 

Find and control paths 

Shortest paths with ANY SHORTEST 

When several paths connect two entities, many applications need one shortest path rather than every possible path. ANY SHORTEST makes that intent explicit. This is useful for dependency analysis, recommendations, network routing, and investigations where fewer intermediate steps are preferred. 

MATCH ANY SHORTEST ({id: 1})->{,2}(d) RETURN d.id AS dst

Quantified edge patterns 

Quantified edge patterns repeat a complete relationship pattern and can apply conditions to intermediate nodes. In the following example, each repeated step requires the source person to use Chrome. This gives developers more control than repeating only an edge pattern. 

MATCH p=(a:Person {id: 987})((x)-[k:knows]->() WHERE x.browserUsed = 'Chrome'){2}(b:Person) FOR n IN NODES(p) WITH OFFSET off RETURN n.browserUsed ORDER BY a.id, b.id, off LIMIT 12

Complete path modes 

Path modes define whether a traversal can revisit nodes or edges.  

  • WALK permits repetition.  
  • TRAIL prevents repeated edges. 
  • SIMPLE prevents repeated interior nodes.  
  • ACYCLIC prevents any repeated node.  
  • DIFFERENT EDGES prevent one edge from satisfying more than one edge variable in the match.  

These choices help query results reflect the meaning of a route, hierarchy, or dependency chain. 

MATCH WALK (:Person {firstName: "Juliana"})-[:studyAt]->(:University)<-[:studyAt]-(p:Person) RETURN p.firstName AS name MATCH TRAIL (:Person {firstName: "Juliana"})-[:studyAt]->(:University)<-[:studyAt]-(p:Person) RETURN p.firstName AS name MATCH SIMPLE (x)->{2}(y) RETURN COUNT(*) AS path_count MATCH ACYCLIC (x:`node` {id: 1})->(y)->(z) RETURN x.id, y.id, z.id ORDER BY x.id, y.id, z.id MATCH DIFFERENT EDGES (p:Person {name: 'Keanu Reeves'})-[e:ACTED_IN]->(m:Movie) RETURN m.title AS movie

Unbounded variable-length path patterns 

Variable-length paths previously required a maximum hop count. Unbounded quantifiers allow the graph structure to determine the traversal depth when no meaningful fixed limit exists. The example follows one or more relationships, while ACYCLIC prevents the traversal from visiting the same node twice. Unbounded refers to the path expression, not unlimited compute, so use selective starting points and test performance with representative graph density. 

MATCH ACYCLIC ()-[]->{1,}() RETURN COUNT(*) AS total

Inspect paths and graph elements 

NODES, EDGES, and INNER_NODES 

These functions expose the contents of a matched path. NODES returns all nodes in the path, EDGES returns all relationships in the path, and INNER_NODES returns the intermediate nodes without the endpoints. Applications can use these results to explain lineage, dependencies, and investigative findings instead of returning only a destination. 

MATCH p=({id: 1})-[]->{0,4}(z) RETURN NODES(p) AS res_nodes, INNER_NODES(p) AS res_inner_nodes ORDER BY z.id

ELEMENT_ID 

ELEMENT_ID returns the identity of a graph element. It is useful when an application must compare, track, or reference a specific node or edge independently of its business properties. 

MATCH (x) RETURN ELEMENT_ID(x) AS vid, x AS actual_id ORDER BY x.id LIMIT 5

SOURCE and DESTINATION 

SOURCE and DESTINATION identify the endpoints of an edge. This makes directional checks and edge-centric analysis easier, especially when a query starts from a relationship rather than a node. 

MATCH (x)-[e]->() RETURN x.id, SOURCE(e).id AS s ORDER BY e.src, e.dst LIMIT 10 MATCH ()-[e]->(x) RETURN false IN COLLECT_LIST(x = DESTINATION(e)) AS no

Compose larger queries 

NEXT 

NEXT passes the output of one query stage into the next, allowing analysts to express a multistep question in a single query. For example, they can calculate a measure, filter the result, traverse another relationship, and summarize the final result without moving intermediate data into application code. 

MATCH (m:Message)-[:hasCreator]-(p:Person) RETURN p, AVG(m.length) AS avg_msg_length GROUP BY p NEXT FILTER avg_msg_length > 100u MATCH (p)-[:knows]->(:Person) RETURN avg_msg_length, COUNT(*) AS connections GROUP BY p, avg_msg_length

EXISTS subqueries 

EXISTS answers a yes-no question about another graph pattern. It can filter rows or participate inside an aggregate without requiring the outer query to return the matching details. 

MATCH (x) WHERE EXISTS { MATCH (y) WHERE y.id = 5 RETURN y } RETURN x.id AS xid ORDER BY xid MATCH (x) RETURN COUNT(*) FILTER ( WHERE EXISTS { MATCH (x)-[]->(y) RETURN y } ) AS count_with_out

CALL subqueries 

CALL runs a contained query for each current outer result. In the example, it calculates each node’s outgoing degree and returns that value with the node identifier, keeping the intermediate calculation contained within the query. 

MATCH (x) CALL { MATCH (x)-[e]->(y) RETURN COUNT(e) AS out_degree } RETURN x.id AS xid, out_degree ORDER BY xid

OPTIONAL CALL 

OPTIONAL CALL preserves the outer row when the contained query has no match. This supports enrichment scenarios where related information is useful but not required. 

MATCH (x {id: 1}) OPTIONAL CALL { MATCH (y)-[]->(x) RETURN y.id AS yid } RETURN x.id AS xid, yid ORDER BY yid

UNION DISTINCT 

UNION DISTINCT combines compatible result sets and removes duplicate rows. It complements UNION ALL, which preserves duplicates, so the query can choose the correct set behavior. 

MATCH () LIMIT 3 RETURN 42 AS x UNION MATCH () LIMIT 3 RETURN 100u AS x

Summarize connected data

Filtered and paged aggregates 

Filtered aggregates calculate a summary over a selected subset. Paging controls such as LIMIT can be applied within the aggregate, giving developers precise control over which values contribute to the result. 

MATCH (m:Movie) RETURN COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE m.released < 1980 LIMIT 10) AS filtered_count

Nested aggregations 

Nested aggregation supports layered questions, such as finding the minimum of averages calculated across groups or paths. This reduces the need to move intermediate results into application code. 

MATCH (a:`node`)-[e:`edge`]->{1,2}(b:`node`) RETURN a.id AS id, MIN(AVG(e.weight)) AS min_average GROUP BY id

COLLECT_ONE, COLLECT_LIST, and COLLECT_ELEMENTS 

Collection functions retain values or graph elements for evaluation as a group. COLLECT_ONE selects one value, COLLECT_LIST builds a list, and COLLECT_ELEMENTS gathers graph elements. They are useful for path-level checks, ordered output, and analysis across repeated relationships. 

MATCH (p:`node` {id: 1})-[e]->{2}(p1:`node` {id: 1}) RETURN (COLLECT_ONE(e.weight) IN [e[0].weight, e[1].weight]) AS contained MATCH ()-[e]->{1,2}() RETURN COLLECT_LIST(ALL e.weight) AS w ORDER BY w LIMIT 20 MATCH ()-[a:ACTED_IN]->{0,4}() WHERE SIZE(COLLECT_ELEMENTS(DISTINCT a.roles)) > 4 RETURN TO_JSON_STRING(a.roles) AS r

Work with values and text 

Dynamic nested data 

Support for dynamic nested data lets queries work with richer values that do not fit a flat property model. This is useful when graph entities contain structured application payloads, nested attributes, or evolving schemas. 

CAST 

 CAST converts a value to a supported target type. Explicit conversion makes comparisons and calculations more predictable when source data contains different numeric types. 

RETURN CAST(42 AS DOUBLE) AS double_res, CAST(42 AS UINT) AS uint_res, CAST(42.5d AS INT) AS int_res

RANGE 

RANGE creates a numeric sequence. A generated sequence can support iteration, testing, bucketing, and list-oriented calculations within a query. 

RETURN RANGE(0, 4) AS res

POWER 

POWER performs exponent calculations. It extends the numeric expressions available for scoring, weighting, and mathematical transformations. 

RETURN POWER(-2, 3) AS res

NORMALIZE and IS NORMALIZED 

Unicode text can have visually identical but technically different encodings. NORMALIZE converts text to a normalization form, while IS NORMALIZED checks its current form. This supports more consistent matching and grouping across multilingual data. 

RETURN NORMALIZE('cafe\u0301') AS normalized_text RETURN 'cafe\u0301' IS NFKD NORMALIZED AS is_normalized

Regular-expression functions 

The MSFT.REGEXP functions match, count, locate, extract, and replace text patterns. They help prepare identifiers, names, codes, and descriptions before those values are compared or summarized. 

RETURN MSFT.REGEXP_LIKE('café', 'caf.') AS x RETURN MSFT.REGEXP_COUNT('abcabcabc', 'abc') AS n RETURN MSFT.REGEXP_INSTR('hello world', 'world') AS p RETURN MSFT.REGEXP_REPLACE('a1b2c3', '[0-9]', '#') AS s RETURN MSFT.REGEXP_SUBSTR('abc123def', '[0-9]+') AS s

Design guidance 

Use the narrowest pattern that answers the question. Start from selective nodes, specify relationship and node labels, and apply filters early. Use bounded traversal when the business question has a natural maximum. When depth is unknown, combine an unbounded path with an appropriate path mode and test it against representative graph density. Return only the properties or path elements the application requires. 

Feature availability can vary by environment and release stage.  Confirm the release stage and regional availability of each feature before publication. If availability differs by feature, identify the applicable release stage in each section. 

Next steps 

Start with a connected-data scenario such as lineage, dependency analysis, recommendations, investigations, or knowledge discovery. Identify the relationships the question must follow, choose the path mode and traversal depth that match the scenario, and then use composition and aggregation features to shape the result.

fabric_blog:1762eca8130f.title: T-SQL language enhancements in Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse (Preview)
fabric_blog:1762eca8130f.excerpt:
Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse is expanding its T-SQL capabilities with four language enhancements in preview. GROUP BY ALL, ORDER BY ALL, the QUALIFY clause, and the FROM ... SELECT query format help SQL developers and data professionals reduce repetitive code, simplify query maintenance, and make analytical logic easier to understand.

Figure: A T-SQL query uses GROUP BY ALL and ORDER BY ALL in Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse.

What’s new

Four T-SQL language enhancements are available in preview:

  • GROUP BY ALL — automatically groups by every non-aggregate expression in the SELECT list, reducing duplication between SELECT and GROUP BY clauses.
  • ORDER BY ALL — sorts results by each column in the SELECT list, using the same column order, so developers do not need to repeat every sort expression.
  • QUALIFY — filters rows after window functions are evaluated, so common ranking and top-N patterns no longer require an additional subquery or common table expression.
  • FROM ... SELECT — provides an alternative query format that begins with the data source and defines the selected columns later, allowing developers to write complex queries in a source-first sequence.

These additions reduce repetitive code and make query intent easier to understand. They are especially valuable when queries include many grouping or sorting columns, when analytical results require filtering, or when a source-first structure makes complex logic easier to follow and maintain.

Together, these enhancements make queries easier to adapt as requirements change. Developers can add or remove projected columns with less rework, filter analytical results without an extra query layer, and organize complex queries in the sequence that best matches how they reason about the data.

New capabilities:

  • Write shorter queries with less repeated code.
  • Make grouping, ordering, and analytical filtering easier to understand.
  • Reduce maintenance when projected columns change.
  • Express source-first query logic in a clear, natural sequence.
  • Use familiar T-SQL capabilities directly in Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse.

Conclusion

These T-SQL language enhancements make everyday query development in Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse more concise and expressive. Whether you are summarizing data, sorting wide result sets, filtering window-function results, or organizing complex query flows, the new syntax helps you focus on analytical intent instead of repetitive code.

For syntax, supported options, and examples, refer to the documentation for QUALIFY, GROUP BY ALL, ORDER BY ALL, and FROM ... SELECT. As you evaluate these preview capabilities, share your scenarios and feedback with the Microsoft Fabric community on Reddit.

simon_willison:efcf00e7bea3.title: The U.S. Census Bureau and “Super Intelligence”
simon_willison:efcf00e7bea3.excerpt:
I was reminded today of AI Adoption Rate Trending Down for Large Companies, a chart produced by Apollo Global Management in September 2025, which appeared to show a slowdown in U.S. corporate AI adoption based on numbers collected by the U.S. Census Bureau. At the time I used that chart to demonstrate GPT-5 data analysis, and then to experiment with Claude's new Code Interpreter. I decided to try running those numbers again to see what had changed over the past year, and in doing so learned that the Bureau has fallen foul of Executive Order 14434, aka the asinine Super Intelligence one.

First, the updated chart

Every two weeks the U.S. Census Bureau runs a survey called the Business Trends and Outlook Survey (aka BTOS). Each time it goes to 200,000 businesses out of 1.2 million total - the surveyed group (a "panel") cycles such that an individual business only completes the survey every twelve weeks.

The latest data is published on alternating Thursdays at 10am.

I used the most recent numbers (published October 22, 2026) to create a new version (GPT-6 Astra Extra High transcript) of the AI adoption chart, updated to reflect both the last twelve months and a change that was made to the survey question sent out by the Bureau:

For comparison, here's that AI adoption chart from last year (my GPT-5 version):

In September 2025 the largest (250+ employees) companies answered "yes" around 12% of the time to the question about whether they used AI in "producing goods or services".

Under the new "any business function" wording, by February 2026, those same large companies answered "yes" around 30% of the time, and by October 2026 that had increased to around 40%.

The data in the above chart comes from the "Employment size class" XLSX file, available from here. Here's a copy of the file I used.

You can view the survey document that is sent out to businesses - here's my snapshot copy of that 346KB PDF.

The changing language of the questions

As the chart demonstrates, the question asked by the Bureau changed in a material way on November 17th, 2025. Prior to that date, the question they asked was this (emphasis mine):

In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in producing goods or services? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.)

On December 3rd, 2025, the Bureau announced a significant change to that question. Here's the replacement:

In the last two weeks, did this business use Artificial Intelligence (AI) in any of its business functions? (Examples of AI: machine learning, natural language processing, virtual agents, voice recognition, etc.)

No more "producing goods or services" - now it's "in any of its business functions"! This means that the answers to the question before and after November 17th are not directly comparable.

From October 19, 2026, they ask about Super Intelligence

When I went looking for the updated question language in the latest XLSX file, I couldn't find it. I found this instead:

In the last two weeks, did this business use Super Intelligence or SI (formerly referred to as Artificial Intelligence or AI) in any of its business functions? (Examples of SI use include: SI-powered data analysis; generative SI for marketing, product design, or coding; virtual SI agents for customer service; SI-powered forecasting or pricing; SI-driven computer vision for quality control, etc.)

The BTOS about page explains what happened:

Beginning with the October 19, 2026 collection, instrument wording was updated due to Executive Order 14434.

The current numbers reflect the old Artificial Intelligence survey wording - the first survey results reflecting the Super Intelligence wording are due for publication on Thursday.

Is this going to affect the survey?

The obvious open question here is whether this wording change is going to affect the survey results.

The businesses answering this survey will have last seen that question twelve weeks ago, when it was still called AI. Hopefully the new language isn't going to confuse them, especially since the survey helpfully spells out "formerly referred to as Artificial Intelligence or AI".

I can't help but laugh at the absurdity of "SI-powered data analysis; generative SI for marketing, product design, or coding; virtual SI agents for customer service" though.

claude_code_releases:8491ebd6e665.title: v2.1.317
claude_code_releases:8491ebd6e665.excerpt:
What's changed

  • Added a warning to /schedule when a new cloud scheduled task gets connectors you did not ask for, with how to remove them
  • Added a check that asks before a web or shell tool call sends your account email address to the network
  • Added onFailure: "block" for Agent SDK hook callbacks, so a callback that fails blocks the action instead of letting it run
  • Added a notice in Claude Desktop's Code tab when your organization's remote managed settings haven't loaded for the session, and another once they do
  • Added a notice when auto mode's check has no answer for a subagent's tool call, which used to leave nothing in the main view
  • Added anthropic.plan, anthropic.seat_type, anthropic.provider and anthropic.custom_base_url to OTel metrics, events and spans
  • Added a cost report to the Claude apps gateway admin API, GET /v1/organizations/analytics/cost, for reading past spend over a date range in total, per developer, per day or per IdP group
  • Added a daily record of each developer's IdP groups on Claude apps gateways with admin: set, kept for admin.identity_retention_days, which the cost report groups by
  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NESTED_SESSION_ID: set it to 1 on a self-hosted runner to have claude -p run inside a session use that session's ID and transcript, as in earlier versions
  • Fixed project and local MCP servers disconnecting after the first turn in some Claude desktop sessions
  • Fixed auto mode failing every turn when an LLM gateway set as the base URL answers 403 or 422 to its server-side safety check (a 403 with an apiKeyHelper is unchanged)
  • Fixed claude auth status exiting before a slow token refresh was saved, which could sign you out on the next run
  • Fixed a project's effortLevel setting being ignored by sessions that an app starts ahead of time and then opens in the project, such as new sessions in the desktop app's Code tab
  • Fixed claude --from-pr reporting "No conversations found" in projects with many sessions when the linked session was older than the first page
  • Fixed the second of two simultaneous permission prompts showing no file path or command on claude.ai and the mobile apps
  • Fixed Remote Control and SDK hosts offering "don't ask again" on a mod's tool calls
  • Fixed session titles being lost in cloud and SDK sessions when a new message or Stop arrived while the title was generating
  • Fixed self-paced /loop wakeups sometimes not being scheduled when Claude left a field out of its request
  • Fixed auto mode in cloud sessions stopping for approval when the Artifact tool uploaded, wrote to a database or saved a file through the outputs folder
  • Fixed skills synced from claude.ai being lost or downloaded again every ten minutes when they can't be written to disk
  • Fixed /schedule leaving a cloud scheduled task's next run time and link out of its results after creating or updating it
  • Fixed screen readers speaking a running subagent's elapsed time and token count on every change in screen reader mode
  • Fixed a region or network block (HTTP 403) being shown as a sign-in failure; the error now explains the block
  • Fixed Claude saying a working claude.ai connector needed authorization or had failed in cloud sessions when a synced plugin included the same server
  • Fixed claude -p exiting 0 when a full disk or quota lost its transcript or ~/.claude.json writes; it now prints an error and, in text and json output, exits 1. Full NFS exports may be missed
  • Fixed edits to settings files made in the first second or so after launch not taking effect until a settings file changed again
  • Fixed old transcripts not being cleaned up on machines where some runs skip cleanup, such as runs using --setting-sources
  • Fixed deleted agent team inboxes being re-created by a teammate's late message
  • Fixed a re-created agent teammate being removed from its team by an earlier shutdown approval
  • Fixed stored scheduled tasks being impossible to list or delete after scheduled tasks were turned off
  • Fixed Claude deleting your most recently updated /team-onboarding guide when asked to delete one without naming which
  • Fixed Claude saying a /team-onboarding guide was deleted when the server refused the delete
  • Fixed the Claude apps gateway hiding Amazon Bedrock's "Input is too long." error, which left sessions failing every turn with "upstream rejected the request" instead of compacting
  • Fixed self-hosted runner sessions losing recent turns or the whole conversation when restarted while a plan waited for approval
  • Fixed "Prompt is too long" after automatic compaction in sessions whose very large CLAUDE.md changed since it was last sent
  • Fixed high memory use and slow startup in headless sessions with many plugins that register commands
  • Fixed stdio MCP servers receiving an empty AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK when their env config sets it to empty; the variable is now unset, so the server can use the machine's own AWS credentials
  • Fixed API requests failing with "unable to get local issuer certificate" behind some TLS-inspecting proxies after a root certificate renewal
  • Fixed very long conversations losing their earlier summary when compaction had to shorten its own request
  • Fixed a PDF's own metadata being able to make Read and @-mentions under-count its pages
  • Fixed DISABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_OPUS and DISABLE_PROMPT_CACHING_SONNET having no effect on [1m], other-region and undated spellings of the default model
  • Fixed /artifacts and the Artifact tool's shared list showing no shared artifacts when you have 200 or more of your own
  • Fixed Claude treating partial Grep and Glob results as complete when a search hit its time limit
  • Fixed OpenTelemetry exports to an https:// endpoint through a proxy never being sent when they started while another export was still in progress
  • Fixed a flood of connection attempts to a proxy that blocks (HTTP 403) OpenTelemetry exports to an http:// endpoint
  • Fixed OpenTelemetry exports hanging indefinitely behind a proxy that never answers; they now time out after 10 seconds, or OTEL_EXPORTER_OTLP_TIMEOUT up to 30 seconds
  • Fixed resumed sessions telling Claude again about a file change it already knew about
  • Fixed Claude sometimes not using a built-in tool in a resumed session after an earlier call failed because the tool was switched off
  • Fixed /remote-control answering "Unknown command" instead of saying that Remote Control is turned off by the disableRemoteControl setting
  • Fixed agent team teammates in tmux or iTerm2 panes starting in auto mode when the lead session was in manual mode
  • Fixed a background session sometimes losing a just-made change of permission mode when it was upgraded or retired
  • Fixed Ctrl+C stopping all running background agents when pressed to clear typed text at the prompt
  • Fixed /feedback showing "Enter to confirm" while a report is being sent
  • Fixed child processes of a stopped shell command sometimes being sent SIGTERM twice, which could make some programs skip their cleanup
  • Fixed claude -p run inside a cloud or self-hosted runner session sharing that session's ID: it wrote into the session's transcript, and a restart could resume the wrong conversation
  • Fixed claude -p run inside a cloud or self-hosted runner session generating a title of its own and sending it to that session
  • Improved the error shown on Microsoft Foundry when Azure credentials can't be loaded: it now says to check or refresh them, and reports as cloud_credential_error
  • Improved /design-sync to say up front when your design system has moved to Claude, and stop before building instead of failing at upload
  • Improved the startup error when a required Claude apps gateway can't be reached: it points to the network instead of a sign-in, and says when the gateway's TLS certificate can't be verified
  • Improved the "Resume this session with" hint shown at exit to repeat the flags you launched with (for example --chrome --debug) ahead of --resume
  • Improved how self-hosted runners recover from server errors: after a 5xx other than 501 or 529, a runner's next poll now opens a new connection instead of reusing the one that failed
  • Improved how self-hosted runner sessions recover from server errors: after a 5xx other than 501 or 529, a session now opens new connections instead of reusing the one that failed
  • Improved how self-hosted runner sessions recover when connections stop answering: after a heartbeat gets no answer, a session now opens new connections instead of trying each idle one in turn
  • Changed SendMessage so a message to a running background agent arrives earlier: its running command moves to the background, without being stopped
  • Changed subagents and teammates on a different model from the main conversation to use that model's saved effort level or its default, instead of the session's effort level
  • Changed exit to skip the "Background work is running" prompt for plugin monitors
  • Changed the built-in plugin-authoring skill to offer once, after a mod you built works, to help share the mod
  • Removed the Read tool's "file unchanged since your last Read" stub: reading an unchanged file again returns its content
  • Windows: Fixed every tool call being refused on some volumes where the native path lookup fails; the working-directory check now compares the folder's identity instead
  • Windows: Fixed the session scratchpad and other temporary paths growing with your project's path length in sessions not started by Claude Desktop, which made repositories cloned into them hit the 260-character path limit
  • Gateway: Fixed the status line and /usage showing a developer's own spend limit as 100% used after their group's pooled budget ran out
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed Claude not seeing the interrupted tool call when a session moves to a new runner and the turn is older than CLAUDE_CODE_RESUME_INTERRUPTED_TURN_MAX_AGE_MS
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed an MCP server that was switched off coming back on after the session moved to a new machine, when the session service had refused to save the switch
  • Remote Control: Improved fork names when the app doesn't set one: a long name keeps its "(fork)" ending, and in sessions started with claude remote-control a fork of "Name (fork)" is "Name (fork 2)"
  • [VSCode] Fixed forked conversations dropping messages: only one of the tool calls Claude ran in parallel was kept, and the last messages a compaction kept were lost, which could leave Claude's answer without the question it answered
  • [VSCode] Fixed a message being lost when Claude did not finish starting in time: the extension now starts Claude once more before showing the error
  • [VSCode] Fixed the sign-in screen opening when a request is blocked for its region or network

fabric_blog:4ccf04047cf8.title: Bring insights and action together with Fabric Apps in Org apps
fabric_blog:4ccf04047cf8.excerpt:
Business users move from understanding what happened, to investigating why, to acting. Microsoft Fabric can bring that journey together.  Fabric Apps provide purpose-built, data-driven experiences when users need more than a report. Org apps distribute them alongside Power BI reports and other supported Fabric content in a curated destination.

Move from insight to action in one destination

Power BI reports help users monitor performance, explore trends, and understand what’s happening in the business. Many insights, however, lead to a next step: submitting a request, updating a plan, investigating an exception, assigning an owner, or tracking a resolution.

A Fabric App provides the custom interface and workflow for that next step. Including it in an org app places action beside the reports and operational content that provide context. Users enter one destination organized around their role, review the insight, open the Fabric App, and act.

Understanding apps in Fabric

Experience

Purpose

Value

Fabric Apps

Build for a specific task

Create purpose-built applications connected to Fabric data, with managed APIs, authentication, hosting, and service integration.

Org apps

Distribute in business context

Package Fabric Apps with Power BI reports, paginated reports, notebooks, maps, and real-time dashboards, with tailored navigation, branding, and audiences.

Workspace apps

Distribute Power BI content

Package and publish reports and dashboards from a workspace. Does not support notebooks and real-time dashboards, automatically granting and revoking access to underlying items and support for Fabric Git integration

What the combined experience looks like

Consider a retailer that wants regional managers to identify store issues and coordinate a response.  The Store Performance page displays a Power BI report, with other business experiences available through the org app navigation.

Start with the insight

A regional manager opens the Retail Operations Hub, an app designed around the work of running stores. The landing experience surfaces a Power BI report with revenue, margin, inventory, and customer-service trends. A real-time dashboard highlights emerging operational issues.

Figure: Shows a Power BI report with revenue, margin, inventory, and customer-service trends

Continue into a Fabric App

The report shows that a store is missing its sales target while carrying excess inventory. The manager opens the Store Action Planner, a Fabric App included in the same org app. The application brings the relevant context into a focused workflow where the manager can review the exception, choose a response, assign owners, and track the plan.

Figure: The Store Action Planner opens as a dedicated Fabric App page within the Retail Operations Hub.

Keep reporting and actions connected

The org app keeps the solution together while tailoring content for regional and store managers. Business owners can update navigation and included items without rebuilding the Fabric App. Each team retains clear ownership: BI authors evolve reports, developers improve the Fabric App, and business owners curate the org app.

Benefits

  • One place to work: Move from Power BI insight to action without finding another tool.
  • Role-based distribution: Give each audience the right mix of reports, applications, and operational content.
  • Clear ownership: Let BI authors, developers, and business owners evolve their parts independently within one consistent destination.
  • Business context: Organize navigation and branding around the process, not the underlying technology or workspace.

Get started

Build the tailored experience with Fabric Apps, then use the org app guidance to package it with Power BI reports and other supported Fabric content. Build the experience users need with Fabric Apps. Distribute it in the context of their work with org apps.

fabric_blog:5f209baed0bf.title: From a prompt to an operational dashboard: Generate Real-Time Dashboards with Copilot (Preview)
fabric_blog:5f209baed0bf.excerpt:
Start with the question, not a blank dashboard

Which transit stations are sending the most fans toward a stadium? How does that incoming demand compare with activity at the gates? Where are queues building?

Answering these operational questions traditionally requires translating them into tables, queries, visualizations, and a dashboard layout. When you already know what you want to monitor, that setup can get in the way of the question you are trying to answer.

Copilot in Microsoft Fabric can generate a Real-Time Dashboard from a natural-language description of the insights you want. Working with a selected database in an Eventhouse, it uses the tables in that database to create a dashboard tailored to your goal.

Figure: Start generating a Real-Time Dashboard with Copilot from an Eventhouse database.

Rather than beginning with an empty canvas and building each visual separately, you describe the operational view you need. Copilot helps create the initial dashboard, and you review and customize it for your team.

Describe, refine, and create

Copilot can already help you write KQL queries and edit individual dashboard tiles. With dashboard generation, you can start one level higher: describe the operational view you need and let Copilot bring several related insights together into an initial dashboard.

Copilot works from the context you provide about the dashboard you want to create. Describe the operational goal first, then add the details that matter for the view you have in mind. For example, specify the signals you want to monitor, the comparisons that are important, and any tables you know are relevant.

You can also describe how you want the information organized. You might ask for an overview of the most important measures together with trends over time and breakdowns by location. You don't need to define every tile before you start. Use follow-up messages to clarify the request as Copilot develops the dashboard plan.

Before creating the dashboard, review how Copilot has interpreted the request. This gives you an opportunity to narrow the scope, emphasize a particular comparison, or add context that was missing from the original prompt.

From your Eventhouse, open New Real-Time Dashboard and select Generate with Copilot (Preview). In the Copilot pane, describe your goal, the data you want to prioritize, and how you want the dashboard organized. Data-specific example prompts can help you get started.

 

Figure: Describe the operational insights you want in the Copilot pane.

The experience is conversational. You can follow how Copilot interprets your request and use follow-up messages to refine the scope or focus before creating the dashboard. For example, you might clarify which tables matter or ask to emphasize comparisons between locations instead of an overall summary.

When you're ready, select Start dashboard creation, choose a dashboard name and workspace location, and select Create. The result is a Real-Time Dashboard you can continue to edit, not a static image of suggested charts.

Figure: Choose a name and workspace for the generated Real-Time Dashboard

Example: Connect transit arrivals with stadium gate load

Consider a stadium operations team preparing for an event. Transit arrivals provide one view of incoming demand, while gate activity and queue lengths provide another. Looking at those signals together helps the team understand where to focus its attention.

In this example, the prompt points Copilot to the relevant transit, stadium gate, stadium zone, and match-event data. It asks for estimated passengers and fans heading to the stadium, broken down by station and transit line, alongside gate entries and queue lengths. The goal is specific: compare incoming transit demand with activity at stadium entrances.

That level of context makes the desired analysis concrete. The goal isn't simply to visualize every available column. It's to compare people arriving by transit with activity at the stadium entrances.

The generated dashboard brings several views together:

  • Summary tiles for estimated transit passengers, fans heading to the stadium, the relationship between those totals, and average gate queue length.
  • A comparison of transit demand and gate entries over time.
  • Passenger breakdowns by station and transit line.
  • Gate-level and zone-level comparisons of transit inflow and gate activity.
  • A detailed table of current gate load and queues.

Together, these views give the team an overview and a way to inspect individual locations. A summary can suggest where to look next; a station breakdown or gate table provides more detail for that investigation.

As with any generated dashboard, review the result before relying on it for operational decisions. Verify the queries, relationships between the data, and the meaning of the measures to make sure the dashboard represents the intended analysis.

Make the dashboard your own

An initial dashboard gives you something concrete to evaluate. Are the most important measures easy to find? Does each chart answer a clear question? Would a different visual make a comparison easier to understand?

After generation, you can change visual types and modify the queries behind the tiles. Copilot can also help with editing visuals or writing queries as you refine the dashboard.

Figure: The generated dashboard combines transit demand, gate activity, and queue information.

Next steps

Explore Generate Real-Time Dashboard using Copilot for the workflow and use Copilot's feedback controls to share what works and what needs improvement.


Learn how to further Customize Real-Time Dashboard Visuals to make this dashboard your own.

fabric_blog:6d9c0429baf2.title: Data Days: Learn, build, and connect with AI @Work

Real people. Real projects. Real AI on Fabric, SQL, and Power BI.

Data Days goes beyond live sessions. Join a community study group, explore the Fabric Apps Gallery, or put your creativity to the test in the Power BI Dataviz World Championships and community contests.

Have something to share? Host a session, lead a study group, or bring an existing community event into Data Days. Whether you're learning, building, or teaching, there's a place for you.

Want to work toward a certification?

Data Days includes exam preparation, community study groups, and limited certification voucher offers. Eligible participants can explore 100% discount offers for DP-600, DP-700, and DP-800, plus 50% discount offers for select additional exams. Eligibility requirements and deadlines apply.

Come with curiosity. Leave with something you want to try, someone new to learn with, or something you've created yourself.

Explore Data Days today!

dbt_core_releases:0986acfa1a5a.title: v2.0.11
dbt_core_releases:0986acfa1a5a.excerpt:
2.0.11

Released November 03, 2026

Features

  • Add support for BigQuery query reservation configuration at model and connection levels (#15486)
  • Report whether each node ran remotely, locally, or on Lake Compute in anonymous usage telemetry.
  • Show a determinate progress bar for the parse phase in interactive terminals, matching the render/analyze/run experience, and name the stage in progress (building model nodes, resolving data tests, typechecking macros) during the stretches where no assets are being parsed, plus a progress indicator while the semantic manifest is validated, so the console no longer looks idle
  • Rename the --run-cache-mode CLI flag to --state-mode to match the dbt State terminology it configures. --run-cache-mode is kept as a deprecated alias and will keep working, with a warning, until it is removed in a future release.
  • Add state configuration to ignore external modifications on model target tables/views (only implemented for views to begin with)
  • Support the allow_jinja_file_extensions project flag, so resource files may carry a trailing Jinja suffix (model.sql.j2, doc.md.j2) (#16296)
  • Add telemetry for state selector operations to track performance and usage of modified/new/unmodified node selection
  • Support authenticated private S3 downloads for dbt update manifests and binaries.
  • Add DBT_CLOUD_LOGIN_HOST (and optional DBT_CLOUD_LOGIN_ACCOUNT_ID) so dbt login can authenticate through an account host's /oauth/authorize instead of the registration page, for SSO accounts the registration page cannot route.
  • [docs v2] Add resource filter to lineage view to select what resource types are displayed in the DAG
  • Add a feature flag registry with --feature NAME[=VALUE] and DBT_ENGINE_FEATURES for setting unstable features; behavior flags and the git deps fast path now resolve through it with unchanged defaults
  • Add the ThreadPoolWait telemetry span for runtime pool queue waits, superseding ConnectionLimitWait
  • Report individual microbatch executions as MicrobatchEvaluated spans in telemetry, file logs, and Core-compatible JSON logs, and list them under their model in interactive output
  • Thread pool wait spans now record the unique_id and batch_id of the node or microbatch they belong to
  • Read and publish AWS Databricks Unity Catalog tables through Lake Compute using profile PAT or OAuth M2M credentials. Use canonical lower-case relation names and full-refresh existing models when adopting propagation with mixed-case database or schema names.

Fixes

  • Fix modules.re functions silently dropping keyword arguments (flags=, maxsplit=, count=) (#15508)
  • Emit only changed columns in Databricks column-tag alter diffs (#16246)
  • Emit only changed keys in Databricks relation-tag SET TAGS diffs (#16248)
  • Emit only changed Databricks column-tag keys in ALTER COLUMN SET TAGS diffs (#16272)
  • Implement TableRepr methods index_of_value_in_column and count_occurrences_of_value_in_column to fix Fusion panic in dbt_utils.get_query_results_as_dict()
  • Copy config.group onto the top-level group for source and singular tests, matching dbt-core (#15930)
  • Snowflake interactive_table: correct the dbt1005 message for an invalid cluster_by — every entry must be non-blank, not just one
  • Make insert_gateway_label idempotent so gateway host resolution no-ops when the label is already present, instead of relying on a caller-side guard
  • Set tags on operation nodes so on-run-start/on-run-end hooks are discoverable when running dbt-core with --use-v2-parser (#16310)
  • Allow integer attribute in the sort, join, unique, and groupby Jinja filters (e.g. sort(attribute=0)), matching Jinja2 behavior
  • Match BigQuery snapshot check columns without regard to case to avoid false row changes.
  • Keep the existing Databricks table when a view model that replaces it fails to build without use_materialization_v2 (#16476)
  • A unit test that overrides one package macro (my_package.my_macro in overrides.macros) no longer makes the package's other macros undefined, matching dbt-core (#16477)
  • Support exposure in the list command's --resource-type option (#16224)
  • Require matching existing and target relation types for Databricks view_update_via_alter updates (#16538)
  • Fix a panic when the project directory is on a Windows network share (UNC path or mapped network drive) (#16428)
  • Unit tests with overrides.vars no longer drop project vars; overrides layer over --vars like dbt Core
  • var.has_var now also reports vars passed with --vars, matching dbt Core
  • Sidecar: Fixed interpolated values for getting relation info
  • docs-v2 source detail page showed the first table's description instead of the source's own
  • Refresh an account-scoped OAuth session when a server rejects an access token before its cached expiry.
  • Validate refreshed OAuth credentials against the cached account and host before persisting.
  • Preserve Snowflake nested JSON fixture escapes and heterogeneous array values during local execution.
  • Commit a rebuilt metadata index only once every table has been written, so a write that fails partway through leaves the previous index in place instead of a mix of new and stale files.
  • Add copy_grants support to Snowflake dynamic tables
  • Find user-installed dbt executables and Windows virtual environments reliably.
  • Fix the Downloading relations progress bar rendering as a stuck 0/N bar. Adapters with no per-item progress reporting now render a spinner instead; Snowflake now reports real per-schema progress so its bar fills as expected
  • Replace DBT_AI_PROVIDER with DBT_ENGINE_AI_PROVIDER (#16312)
  • The environment variables behind --generate-info-schema and --info-schema-dir are now DBT_ENGINE_GENERATE_INFO_SCHEMA and DBT_ENGINE_INFO_SCHEMA_DIR. They were named DBT_GENERATE_INFO_SCHEMA and DBT_INFO_SCHEMA_DIR, outside the reserved DBT_ENGINE_ prefix that the engine's other variables use. The flags themselves are unchanged.
  • Setting DBT_ENGINE_AI_PROVIDER no longer aborts the invocation. The variable was moved onto the reserved DBT_ENGINE_ prefix without being registered as a known engine variable, so validate_engine_env_vars rejected it as user-authored and every command that reached setup exited 1 with dbt1005.
  • Support credential-independent profile metadata and scoped environment values while preserving secret access rules.
  • Match BigQuery partition fields case-insensitively when inspecting existing tables (#14646)
  • Accept compute_region and legacy dataproc_region together in BigQuery profiles.
  • Populate complete query tags for Databricks seeds; fix materialization type for seeds to be seed rather than table (#15931)
  • BigQuery unit tests no longer leak partition pseudocolumns into expected results (#15357)
  • Fix broken image links in documentation (#16288)
  • Protect Windows process environment variables from project .env overrides.
  • Replace deprecated DuckDB single-arrow lambdas with Python-style lambda syntax.
  • Reuse cached relation metadata when checking stale views during development cloning.
  • Honor valid dbt Core-generated package lock checksums for common package declarations with best-effort compatibility.
  • Correct how dbt State classifies model materializations: materialized views submit as VIEW, adapter-specific materializations such as dynamic tables and metric views submit as DBT_CUSTOM (and are therefore no longer eligible as clone candidates), semantic views are no longer submitted, and full-refreshed snapshots submit as FULL
  • Databricks: include all models in catalog.json for schemas with more than 50 relations (#15795)
  • Report the effective dbt State defer-to target, honoring a target's defer_to_target, instead of always reporting the default.
  • Order a unit test's render after the seed that materializes an overlapping source, so dbt build no longer reads the relation before the seed has created it. This ordering now also holds when the tested model is not selected, for example when only the seed and the unit test are selected
  • Preserve BigQuery GEOGRAPHY, TIMESTAMP, and JSON types in dbt OSS unit test fixtures (#16410)
  • Exempt ad-hoc inline (preview) nodes from the model access check, so dbt show --inline and dbt compile --inline can ref() a private or protected model
  • Fix Redshift OAuth authentication failures with an updated ADBC driver.
  • Add new STRUCT and ARRAY columns to BigQuery snapshot tables with their SQL types instead of RECORD or the array's element type (#16350)
  • Keep the microbatch event-time filter on relations derived from a ref with include(), quote(), replace_path(), incorporate() or without_identifier() (#16383)
  • Refresh persisted unit-test given fixture schemas so warehouse DDL changes are reflected.
  • Send Redshift's case-sensitive sqlglot dialect setting to the server when enable_case_sensitive_identifier is enabled
  • Fix DuckDB seeds defined in packages failing to load because the CSV path duplicated the package directory.
  • Add duckdb__date dispatch macro so dbt.date() / dbt.date_spine() work on DuckDB targets
  • Retry transient Redshift query-execution errors (catalog races, serialization conflicts) on the same connection
  • Warn on missing persist_docs columns for Databricks table, incremental, materialized view, and streaming table; fix V2 column comments being gated on the wrong persist_docs config key
  • Snowflake incremental models on catalog-linked databases (e.g. Glue) no longer fail on DROP TABLE ... CASCADE of the __dbt_tmp relation
  • Time Machine replay: rebuild the relations of a recorded list_relations_in_parallel result instead of replaying every listed schema as empty, so --defer no longer treats nodes present in the dev schema as absent and re-points their refs at the deferred relation
  • Time Machine replay now preserves Snowflake column precision/scale (e.g. NUMBER(38,6), TIMESTAMP_LTZ(6)) so unit-test fixture SQL matches the recording
  • Finalize invocation telemetry when execution ends even if background workers retain descendant spans.
  • Fix DuckDB and Databricks incremental/snapshot builds panicking with an unhandled Arrow BinaryView type on BLOB/binary columns (#16364)
  • Include the underlying cause in package hub and tarball request errors, and stop reporting a 500 status when no response was received
  • Auto-exposures discovered from BI tools now carry the target's adapter instead of defaulting to Snowflake, so non-Snowflake projects no longer fail selection with dbt1005 'selected nodes need adapters the target does not declare'
  • Stop emitting the with connection clause for BigQuery Iceberg tables using lakehouse_catalog (LRC) when use_catalogs_v2 is left at its default.
  • Inline SQL and CSV unit-test fixture file contents into the parsed manifest and resolve fixtures in dependency packages. (#16354)
  • Respect project-level overrides of create_schema and other adapter macros invoked from Rust. (#16346)
  • Avoid unsafe CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE operations in BigQuery incremental and snapshot materializations. (#15953)
  • Fix BigQuery incremental models being recreated instead of merged when a concurrent table drop makes a dataset listing fail
  • Skip per-table metadata when hydrating the BigQuery relation cache through ADBC GetObjects. (#16425)
  • BigQuery freshness checks are now faster and safer. Freshness scans for different schemas now run at the same time. Freshness checks for the same schema and different nodes now share one request.
  • Strip CR and BOM from PEM-headered Snowflake private keys so keys saved with Windows line endings decode correctly (#15107)
  • Snowflake seeds now honor the transient config instead of silently creating a permanent table
  • Fetch the tested model's schema for incremental unit tests with static analysis enabled instead of failing with dbt9002
  • Process explainer GetExplainMessage requests in batches.
  • Preserve BigQuery decimal and nested types in unit test fixtures (#16440)
  • Correct the dbt show --info help text, which still said a prior --generate-info-schema run was required
  • DuckDB unit test fixtures for TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE columns are no longer cast to a naive timestamp, which previously dropped the offset and shifted the value by the session timezone (#16470)
  • Fix dbt-dist recursion on version manager shims (#16537)
  • Fix --write-index and --dirty runs missing files added since the last parse: new models, seeds, macros and other resources are now loaded, --dirty selects newly added SQL models and analyses, and --no-partial-load now turns off the cached-state shortcut.
  • Honor OS-assigned loopback ports in OAuth authorization and token-exchange callback URLs.
  • Recognize $$...$$ dollar-quoted strings in the Databricks SQL lexer so a ; inside a metric view's YAML body (e.g. in a comment: block) no longer truncates the compiled create or replace view DDL. (#16385)
  • Return an empty column list when Databricks get_columns_in_relation targets a missing hive_metastore relation (#16472)
  • Clarify the warning for a package-lock.yml written by an older dbt version and point to dbt deps
  • Removed lingering 'dbt' naming from parse-failure and warn_error_options log output, and pointed the parse-failure suggestion at the dbt v2 upgrade guide.
  • Bring Databricks macros in line with dbt-databricks v1.12.4
  • Fix nil pointer dereference panic in BigQuery foundry driver
  • Add ability to record seeds as transient table types for Snowflake
  • Convert Arrow FixedSizeList values to Jinja so Snowflake VECTOR columns do not panic when read into an agate table.
  • Databricks Python models: wait for the all-purpose cluster to be running before creating the execution context, surface Command API error messages, and stop warning on an unset timeout
  • Bump lake compute driver to enable jwt authentication users to no longer need a background pat to be generated.
  • Repeating a single-value flag such as --target or --debug keeps the last value instead of failing with a usage error, matching dbt Core.
  • Send allow_clones, is_defer_to_profile, and defer_enabled on dbt State submit requests for explainer parity
  • [Redshift] Fix issues with external OAuth breaking for multi-threaded execution (#15555)
  • Write warn_error_options to run_results.json args, matching dbt Core.
  • Databricks: views and metric views under an iceberg catalog no longer fail with 'materialized must be incremental, table, or seed' when catalogs.yml v2 is enabled. (#16474)
  • Stop panicking on Jinja AgateTable comparisons; compare tables by identity like dbt 1.x (#15920)
  • Fix model.resource_type returning model for all resource types during parse (#16637)
  • Build source relations the same way as source(), so they skip the adapter's max identifier length check (matching dbt Core) and use catalog_name as the database
  • Fix BigQuery table models being dropped before every rebuild when a cluster_by entry is backtick-quoted or differs in letter case from the stored column
  • Restore connection wait telemetry for runtime pool contention on task operations.
  • Include semantic_manifest.json in the artifact ingest upload when the run writes it
  • A microbatch model's idle time and duration no longer overcount waits of its concurrent batches; the model is idle only while none of its batches runs
  • After a concurrent microbatch batch fails, batches not yet started are canceled instead of running after their model has failed
  • Verify TLS certificates against the operating system's certificate store instead of a bundled CA list, so HTTPS connections work behind TLS-inspecting proxies whose CA is only installed in the OS store.
  • Always mark reused passing dbt State tests as reused in run results.

Under the Hood

  • Refresh README with a dbt v2.0 DAG screenshot stored in assets/ and point the CI badge at the current dbt-labs/dbt workflow.
  • Allow metadata freshness checks to use an explicit artifact directory.
  • Allow base Jinja context builders to reuse a caller-provided ResultStore.
  • Log a warning naming the relation when no schema is returned for a dangling source during static analysis hydration, instead of skipping it silently.
  • Reuse the parsed Jinja AST when extracting unrendered config() arguments.
  • Extend package metadata with cross-project environment routing fields.
  • dbt-parser: avoid a second, redundant Jinja parse when statically recovering source() calls hidden in a conditional branch during model, function, and singular data test rendering
  • Add a per-resource-type applicability table for adapter-specific config keys, replacing the shared WarehouseSpecificNodeConfig field list with per-(resource type, key) status. A key set on a resource type that does not support it now emits a DeprecatedConfigKey warning. On schema.yml and inline config() the key is still applied, so behavior is unchanged; in dbt_project.yml, where the key has no field to deserialize into and already warned, it is dropped.
  • Time Machine replay pins the Jinja wall clock to the recording start, so wall-clock-derived SQL (e.g. a utcnow()-based var) matches the recorded text
  • Add force closing of span subtrees to dbt-tracing, ending a span's structured telemetry even while other handles to it or its descendants are alive.
  • docs-v2: document the overview landing-page customization block in the README
  • Ignore flags: in installed packages' dbt_project.yml: project flags, including behavior change and adapter behavior flags, only apply from the root project

Dependencies

  • Update ADBC drivers to Snowflake 0.21.21, BigQuery 0.21.23, BigQuery Foundry 0.1.11, Databricks 0.21.15, Redshift 0.18.11, Spark 0.1.4, DuckDB Extended 0.0.32, Lake Compute 0.1.13, and MSSQL 1.7.1 (dbt build suffixes).

Security

  • Harden Databricks logged-SQL credential redaction: match credential and encryption clauses case-insensitively, redact every clause rather than only the first, and correctly handle option values containing commas, newlines, quotes or escaped quotes and keys containing dots. (#16053)
  • Checks and dbt show --info/--inline now run in a DuckDB database that can read only the project metadata: no other files, no network access, and no extension installs
  • Upgrade gix to 0.84.0 to address security advisories in the gix dependency family.
  • Update BigQuery and Spark ADBC driver builds to Go 1.26.10.
  • Update rustls-webpki to 0.103.16 and webpki-root-certs to 1.0.10 to reject distrusted certificate chains.
