claude_code_releases:6385d8e47a02.title: v2.1.318
claude_code_releases:6385d8e47a02.excerpt:
What's changed

  • Added a record of your answer when Claude Code asks to turn on the mods it writes in a session
  • Added assume_role on mantle upstreams of the Claude apps gateway, for a role in another AWS account and for per-developer AWS cost attribution
  • Added an effort option to a mod's $.model.fork, so a quick side job can run at low whatever effort the session uses; the result reports the effort sent
  • Added the date a stored claude.ai sign-in ends to claude auth status (loginExpiresAt) and to claude -p JSON results (credential_expires_at)
  • Added a one-line stderr warning to claude -p text output, starting 10 days before a stored claude.ai sign-in ends
  • Fixed --continue sometimes losing the earlier conversation after a malformed tool call's retries ran out (regression in 2.1.314)
  • Fixed macOS sessions with many running Bash commands stalling while memory grew
  • Fixed permission prompts being answered by keys typed just after sending a message, or before a slow prompt appeared
  • Fixed /logout, claude auth logout and claude mcp remove reporting success, and changes to trust, consent or MCP settings being dropped with no word, when the config file could not be updated on a shared network home directory
  • Fixed jobs exiting with Not logged in when another terminal or host signs in again to the same account and organization on the same home
  • Fixed claude mcp add and remove writing the config without its lock: they now wait for it or exit 1, though another job's save can still replace a saved server
  • Fixed claude plugin commands exiting before a slow token refresh was saved, which could sign you out on the next run
  • Fixed claude plugin validate passing a custom-named marketplace file that claude plugin marketplace add rejects
  • Fixed stdio MCP servers that exit on the version probe being re-probed on every start; a server that dies in under 3s for its own reason is also pinned to the legacy handshake for 7 days
  • Fixed sessions being refused at startup by an allowedProviders list that another login on the same machine had stored
  • Fixed idle compaction replacing a conversation with a reply that was not a summary
  • Fixed the "Now using usage credits" notice reappearing about every 30 seconds while a background subagent is running
  • Fixed custom slash commands that fail, or that only Claude can invoke, printing nothing in claude -p and SDK sessions
  • Fixed claude -p and Agent SDK sessions reporting success when an API error cut off a reply while a mod hooked turn.step
  • Fixed a message sent right after a model change still running after Stop in headless sessions: Stop now cancels or stops it as it would a queued message
  • Fixed a deleted session transcript being re-created with its last prompt when an idle non-interactive session exited
  • Fixed claude remote-control hosts, the background daemon and self-hosted runners failing to start new sessions (spawn ENOENT) after an update or version cleanup removed the binary of a still-running process
  • Fixed a running Claude Code process owned by another user (for example one left by sudo claude) being treated as dead by version cleanup, which could delete its binary
  • Fixed /remote-control showing a session as available after a failed connection
  • Fixed /design revoke reporting success when the request failed with a 404
  • Fixed a shell command approved after a self-hosted runner or cloud session restart running in the session's start folder, not the folder it was asked in; if that folder can't be entered, it is not run
  • Fixed Claude not being told when an approved connector tool was unavailable after a cloud session restart
  • Fixed cloud sessions being stopped in the middle of a turn when the service refuses uploads for several minutes
  • Fixed variables a Setup hook writes to CLAUDE_ENV_FILE not reaching the Bash tool in some cloud sessions
  • Fixed the iPhone app showing a cloud session's turn as finished while it kept running, after a response was cut off at a tool call or a refused image or document was removed
  • Fixed a restarted session re-sending a message that failed with an API error, ahead of the newer message waiting behind it
  • Fixed a restarted session dropping its interrupted turn when the restart came right after Claude read a large image or retried a tool call
  • Fixed every connection failing when the NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS file is empty, not PEM, or starts with a damaged certificate: readable certificates are now used, with a warning on stderr
  • Fixed workflows re-running finished agents when resumed after a usage limit
  • Fixed /mcp in cloud sessions counting tools the model can't use; a server's row now shows how many of its tools are available
  • Fixed a duplicate notification when Claude left the status field out of a PushNotification call
  • Fixed the error for a too-large image in a request with more than 20 images always saying the limit was 2000px; it now shows the API's limit
  • Fixed the runtime in background shell details not updating while the dialog is open
  • Fixed a mod's turn.step hook making a stopped reply finish as a success in headless runs
  • Fixed retention cleanup leaving a home that only runs claude -p with no ~/.claude.json backup: it now takes a fresh backup before deleting the last good one
  • Fixed the stored login being replaced by an empty file when a network home directory has no room left for data but still takes new files
  • Fixed tokens from setup-token being refused at start on machines with forceLoginOrgUUID, when the token belongs to a permitted organization
  • Fixed non-interactive launches replacing a ~/.claude.json that isn't valid JSON with defaults; the start now fails, says how to restore the file, and leaves it as is (#87551)
  • Fixed an empty ~/.claude.json with no backup being reported as corrupted; Claude Code now starts as it does when the file is missing
  • Fixed the restore command printed for a damaged or missing ~/.claude.json naming an empty or cut-off backup, or failing on a read-only file
  • Fixed the sign-in failure when a stored claude.ai login reaches its time limit: it now says so, and in claude -p names claude auth login and claude setup-token
  • Improved how ~/.claude.json, settings files and the stored login survive saves on shared network home directories: they are less often deleted, briefly emptied or replaced by a near-empty or older copy
  • Improved sessions on network file systems to look again when the configuration file is wrongly reported as missing, so fewer start without your MCP servers and trusted folders
  • Improved MCP tool errors: a call made before the tool is loaded now returns its input schema
  • Improved the reliability of git commits and pull request creation when the Bash tool runs macOS's built-in /bin/bash
  • Improved "Ask your admin for more usage" in the usage limit menu to send the request in one step
  • Improved how fast remote sessions reconnect after a pause or sleep
  • Improved You should know toasts to say "try again" instead of "press 2", which only works in the terminal
  • Improved auto-update reliability: a brief network failure while verifying a release is now retried right away instead of waiting for the next check
  • Improved unattended runs (claude -p, SDK apps) to stop rewriting ~/.claude.json on every run when nothing in it changed
  • Changed Claude Code to no longer install or update the IDE extension when started in an IDE terminal; use /ide from an outside terminal or your editor's extensions view
  • Changed subagents to stop instead of switching models when "Switch models when a message is flagged" is set to "Ask each time"
  • Changed background subagents to move a shell command to the background after 3 minutes on all providers, so the prompt cache doesn't expire while it runs
  • Changed subagent progress summaries on Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry, or with telemetry off: on a cold prompt cache, one can now wait up to 5 minutes for the subagent's pending response
  • Changed what a mod attaches at prompt.submit to stay in the user's turn rather than go out as a system message
  • Changed deniedMcpServers URL entries to also block Anthropic-provided servers whose upstream URL matches, and connectors in cloud sessions and on self-hosted runners, where the session is given the connector's own URL; otherwise deny a connector by name
  • Changed the /permissions rule details, built-in rules and delete confirmation views to use the standard dialog; pressing Ctrl+C twice there now goes back or cancels instead of quitting
  • Changed /claude-api managed-agents-onboard to give a new agent's built-in tools, and a quickstart template's MCP tools, the auto permission policy ("Judge risky actions") by default, matching the Claude Console; say "run without asking" to opt out
  • Removed the 2.1.288 fix that kept the model's earlier thinking when resuming a conversation started on 2.1.286 or earlier; that thinking can now be dropped
  • Gateway: Added a log warning when the Google access token from a federation (external_account) credentials file is about to expire
  • Gateway: Improved the log hints about listen.trusted_proxies: they now say to list only a proxy that adds the connecting address to X-Forwarded-For itself
  • Gateway: Improved the warning when AWS CountTokens fails on Amazon Bedrock: it says Claude Code, not the gateway, counts after the 501, and points at IAM only when AWS denies access
  • Self-hosted runner: Added CLAUDE_RUNNER_SPAWN_REASON to the orchestrator's spawn-runner hook environment: why Anthropic sent the request (e.g. runner_lost, resumed); unset when none was sent
  • Self-hosted runner: Added a startup warning when --release-idle-session-min is the last argument with no value (still ignored) or has a value of only spaces (still read as 0)
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed the orchestrator's log lines: ok session=… now prints at every log level on stdout (was debug only, stderr) with reason=… after jti=…, and nack session=… ends its fields with reason=… after retryable=…; update scripts that match retryable=true: or retryable=false:
  • Remote Control: Fixed a misleading "spawn error: ENOENT" when a session's working folder is missing; the error now names the folder
  • Remote Control: Improved the title a fork of a terminal fork is created with when the app doesn't set one: "Name (fork 2)"
  • [VSCode] Fixed a window whose sign-in the organization's settings refuse starting a new Claude Code process in the background every minute
  • [VSCode] Fixed a long word in the chat panel's error banner pushing its close button out of view
  • [VSCode] Improved the sign-in screen to show what Claude Code printed when its sign-in status check fails
  • [Cloud sessions] Added a No repository option: a cloud session on an Anthropic-hosted environment can now start without picking a repository
  • [Cloud sessions] Added the usual Chrome names to cloud sessions, so tools other than Playwright can find the built-in Chromium through google-chrome and CHROME_PATH
  • [Cloud sessions] Added a New session button to the card shown when a cloud session's environment was deleted, where the message box is hidden
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed reading GitHub Actions logs in cloud sessions: gh run view --log and gh api log requests now get the log in most environments, not an unreachable redirect
  • [Cloud sessions] Improved most Create PR failure messages in cloud and Remote Control sessions: they now give the reason or a link to GitHub instead of saying Try again
  • [Cloud sessions] Changed connector search results to tell Claude that the search covers only part of the connector directory
  • [Remote Control] Fixed side-by-side checkouts of one repository looking identical in the environment menu's Remote Control rows; each now shows its own folder name
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed keyboard focus and screen reader announcements in Claude Tag admin setup; pressing Escape in the connect form no longer also closes the Add dialog
  • [Code Review] Improved the Code Review analytics page to retry once after a server or network failure, then show a Try again banner instead of empty cards

fabric_blog:225ab7984001.title: Announcing support for Materialized views and streaming tables in Mirrored Azure Databricks catalog
fabric_blog:225ab7984001.excerpt:
Access more Unity Catalog objects through the existing mirrored catalog experience in Microsoft Fabric

We are expanding Mirrored Azure Databricks catalogs in Microsoft Fabric to support materialized views and streaming tables alongside tables.

These objects remain created and managed in Azure Databricks, while Fabric provides read-only access to the underlying data through shortcuts. This brings more of your Unity Catalog environment into Fabric without copying or replicating the data.

What's new

A Mirrored Azure Databricks catalog can now include support:

  • Tables
  • Materialized views
  • Streaming tables

When configuring the mirrored catalog, select the Unity Catalog catalogs, schemas, and supported objects you want to make available in Fabric. Fabric mirrors the selected catalog structure and creates shortcuts to the underlying data.

This enhancement uses the existing Mirrored Azure Databricks catalog item and configuration workflow. There is no separate Fabric item type for materialized views or streaming tables.

Why this matters

Materialized views store precomputed results that can simplify recurring analytical queries. Streaming tables continuously process incoming data and maintain updated results for scenarios that require fresher information. Both object types can play an important role in the datasets that organizations publish for analytics and reporting.

Supporting these objects in a mirrored catalog gives Fabric users access to more of the curated data already available in Azure Databricks. It also allows platform teams to preserve clear ownership: Azure Databricks remains responsible for creating and processing the source objects, while Fabric provides experiences for discovering and analyzing the available data.

Prepare objects for external access

Before a materialized view or streaming table can appear in Fabric, configure it for external data access in Azure Databricks, complete the applicable prerequisites, and grant the required Unity Catalog permissions to the identity used by Fabric. Then refresh or synchronize the mirrored catalog.

Work with data in Fabric

The mirrored catalog includes an automatically generated SQL analytics endpoint for exploring and querying the available data with T-SQL. You can also create a Power BI semantic model and use Direct Lake mode for reporting.

Keep catalog changes in sync

For new mirrors, automatic synchronization of future catalog changes for the selected schema is enabled by default. Supported additions and deletions of schemas, tables, materialized views, and streaming tables can be reflected in Fabric when they meet the configured selection and external-access requirements.

Get started

Follow Tutorial: Configure Microsoft Fabric mirror from Azure Databricks Unity Catalog to create or configure your mirrored catalog. Review Microsoft Fabric Mirrored Catalog from Azure Databricks for prerequisites and external-access guidance.

fabric_blog:6a85cab2008a.title: Adding the Context Streaming Events Need: Reference Data Joins with OneLake Delta Tables in Fabric Eventstream
fabric_blog:6a85cab2008a.excerpt:
Enrich events with business context in real time, enabling faster decisions, more relevant alerts, and lower operational effort downstream. 

A real-time event tells you what happened. Context tells you what it means—and what to do next. In cold-chain logistics, a temperature reading becomes actionable when paired with a shipment’s temperature limits, customer priority, and response contacts. Reference Data Join in Fabric Eventstream brings that context to live events by matching them with business information from Delta tables in OneLake before they reach downstream destinations—so consumers can understand and act on the events without performing separate lookups.

The scenario: Cold chain logistics 

Cold chain logistics moves temperature-sensitive goods, such as fresh produce, dairy, frozen foods, and pharmaceuticals, from origin to destination within strict temperature ranges. Refrigerated trailers, containers, and warehouses must keep products in range at every stage. A few degrees off for too long can spoil a shipment, break compliance requirements, or put patient safety at risk. 

Refrigerated fleet continuously stream sensor telemetry. But a reading alone does not identify the shipment, its temperature limits, or the team responsible for responding. 

An alert without the context

An alert arrives from a refrigerated trailer: "Device TRL-4471 reported 9.2°C." Is the cargo at risk? Which customer is affected? Who should respond? The reading alone can't tell you. 

Figure: A raw temperature alert does not provide enough business context for immediate action.

The missing context --assets, shipments, routes, customers, and response contact already lives in Delta tables in OneLake. Reference Data Join brings that information into Fabric Eventstream before events reach downstream consumers.  

In this illustrative scenario, the trailer carries fresh produce with a configured transport range of 2–8°C for this shipment. A 9.2°C reading is therefore an excursion that operators can assess using the shipment details and assigned response team. 

The pattern is simple: combine live events with business context, then let downstream rules and workflows decide who needs to act.

For example, “TRL-4471: 9.2°C” becomes “Trailer TR-0918: 9.2°C; fresh produce; transport range 2–8°C; Northwind Foods; Tier 1; assigned response contacts.” A downstream rule can compare the reading with the shipment’s limits, flag the excursion, and notify the relevant team. 

The common workaround and tradeoffs 

Reference data can be joined either while events are in motion or after they land in a store. The right choice depends on when the business needs context. 

Land events first, then join for analytics. This approach keeps event payloads lean and avoids duplicating reference attributes on every record. It works well when analysis can wait until the data reaches downstream where it will be enriched. However, it adds a processing step and delays context that stream-based alerts, routing, and automated actions need immediately. 

Enrich events in the stream for time-sensitive scenarios. When alerts, routing, or automated actions must happen in real time, enriching events in motion provides the business context needed to respond immediately. It also creates complete, denormalized events that downstream consumers can use without repeating the join. The trade-off is larger payloads and duplicated reference values, which can increase transport and storage costs and require careful handling as reference data changes. 

For cold-chain monitoring, stream analytics is critical because a temperature excursion can require action before the event reaches storage. Enriching telemetry in Eventstream gives downstream detection and response workflows the cargo limits, customer priority, route, and contact context needed to assess the event immediately. If the use case is historical reporting rather than time-sensitive intervention, joining after ingestion may be the better design. 

 Introducing Reference Data Join In Fabric Eventstream

Reference Data Join lets you join a live stream with reference data stored as Delta tables in OneLake. The reference data appears as its own node on the Eventstream canvas. You join it to your stream inside the pipeline, before the data reaches any destination. 

  • Use OneLake Delta tables. Reuse master data exposed through a Lakehouse, including native tables and shortcuts to data in other workspaces, without copying the data. 
  • Choose no-code or SQL joins. Map keys visually for simple lookups or write SQL for advanced logic. 
  • Select inner or left outer joins. Keep the matching events for downstream processing or preserve every event and flag missing reference data. 
  • Add multiple reference data nodes. Add all the required context to the stream by adding one or more reference data nodes to the topology.  
  • Preview and validate on the canvas. Inspect reference rows and joined output before publishing. 
  • Control columns and refresh intervals. Load only the columns you need and keep slowly changing reference data current by configuring the refresh interval. 

Building the pipeline in few simple steps

Using the cold-chain logistics scenario, we’ll build a real-time pipeline that enriches raw trailer telemetry with Reference Data Join. In this example, an eventstream receives live TrailerTelemetry events from Azure IoT Hub, joined with reference data in Onelake, and sends the enriched records downstream. The following steps show the core pattern; the linked Microsoft Learn guide provides the full setup instructions. 

  1. Add the reference data node. In Edit mode, select Add source and choose Reference Data. A new node appears on the canvas next to your live stream.
Figure: Add a Reference Data source to the Eventstream canvas.
  1. Point it to a Delta table in OneLake. Select the Lakehouse that exposes the reference data, then choose the Delta table you want to use. 

The table can be: 

  • Natively stored in the selected Lakehouse. 
  • A shortcut to a Delta table stored elsewhere in OneLake. 
Figure: Select the Lakehouse that exposes the reference data.Figure: Choose the Delta table to use as the reference source.

3. Load only the columns the pipeline needs and preview the data. After selecting the required columns, open the data preview to confirm the schema and check a few rows. In this illustrative shipment, TRL-4471 carries fresh produce with a specified transport range of 2–8°C for a Tier 1 grocery customer. That makes a 9.2°C reading an excursion requiring prompt assessment.

Figure: Preview the reference-data schema and sample rows before joining.

4. Join it with the default stream. Connect the default stream and the reference node to a join operator. Map the key columns and choose a left outer join when you need to retain readings from devices missing in the reference table; choose an inner join when only matched events should continue. Use the SQL operator for more advanced logic.

Figure: Configure the join between live telemetry and reference data.

5. Test and publish. Preview the enriched output on the canvas, then publish and route it to Eventhouse, Lakehouse, Activator or any other supported destination. As shown in the diagram, you can incorporate multiple reference data sources by chaining Reference Data nodes with join operators.

Figure: Test, publish, and route the enriched stream to downstream destinations.
 

Going further: SQL for advanced logic 

As needs grow, you may want logic beyond a simple lookup. For example, you might calculate an "out of range" flag in the stream and tag each event with the regional hub that covers the trailer's route. 

Add a SQL operator to your Eventstream topology and connect both the reference data nodes and the default stream to the input connector of the SQL operator node as shown in the figure below. Open the SQL operator in edit mode and add the data processing logic. In this example , the query enriches each trailer temperature event with shipment and route-hub details, then writes the result to EnrichedTelemetry. It marks the temperature as EXCURSION when it falls outside the shipment’s allowed range; otherwise, it marks it OK. 

SELECT t.deviceId, t.temperatureC, t.eventTime, a.trailerId, a.cargoType, a.customerName, a.serviceTier, h.hubName, h.onCallContact, CASE WHEN t.temperatureC > a.maxTempC OR t.temperatureC < a.minTempC THEN 'EXCURSION' ELSE 'OK' END AS tempStatus INTO EnrichedTelemetry FROM TrailerTelemetry t LEFT OUTER JOIN TrailerAssets a ON t.deviceId = a.deviceId LEFT OUTER JOIN RouteHubs h ON a.routeId = h.routeId Figure: Reference Data join using SQL operator to add context from multiple tables.

Keeping context fresh

Reference data doesn't stay the same for long. Trailers get reassigned, customers change, and new sensors come online. Set a refresh interval on the reference data node to reload the reference dataset automatically and Eventstream uses the latest snapshot of the table for new lookups. 

The same alert, with context

 

With enrichment in place, the alert now reads: 

"Temperature Alert: Trailer TR-0918 (fresh produce, transport range 2–8°C) at 9.2°C. Customer: Northwind Foods (Tier 1). Hub: Memphis. On call: [contact]."
There is nothing additional to look up and nothing to guess. Within seconds of the reading leaving the trailer, the team knows what's at risk and who to contact.  

Outcome 

What changes 

Faster response 

Alerts arrive with full business context 

One join, many consumers 

The data is enriched once in the stream, and every destination gets the same record 

Lighter device telemetry 

Sensors keep sending small payloads, and metadata stays governed in OneLake 

Figure: The enriched alert provides the business context needed for rapid response.

Beyond cold chain 

The same pattern works anywhere raw events need business context: 

  • Manufacturing: add the asset, production line and maintenance schedule to machine data. 
  • Retail: add product catalog and store details to point-of-sale events. 
  • Aviation: add aircraft type, route and gate to operational events. 
  • Energy and utilities: link meter readings to the customer, rate plan and grid area. 
  • Financial services: tag transactions with account tier and risk profile in real time. 

Get started 

Learn more: Enrich Events with Reference Data in Fabric Eventstreams - Microsoft Fabric | Microsoft Learn

If you find this blog helpful, please give it a thumbs-up! Have ideas for what you'd like to see next? Drop us a comment or reach out to askeventstreams@microsoft.com — we'd love to hear what real-time scenarios you're building and what topics you'd like us to cover in future posts. 

To suggest product improvements or additional capabilities for your scenarios, submit an idea through Fabric Ideas.

fabric_blog:bca544cd94f7.title: OneLake: The file system for agent-first data engineering
fabric_blog:bca544cd94f7.excerpt:
Software engineers are increasingly using agents to build software, and data engineers are no different. We want OneLake to help enable data engineers to develop software in this new agent-first era.

Think about how you work in a terminal: you use it to run programs that read and write files. Both the programs and the data live in the file system. Now apply that model to data engineering: OneLake is the file system, Fabric engines are the programs, and the AI prompt is your terminal.

Over the last few weeks, we’ve released several new capabilities in OneLake that come together to create an experience where agent-first data engineers can thrive. This blog post provides a rundown of those features.

Managing OneLake

OneLake now offers a remotely hosted MCP server (preview), so agents can explore and manage your data without installing a local server. The local MCP option remains available if you prefer. We’ve also added tools to the Fabric Core MCP server for managing shortcuts and OneLake security.

In our previous post, we asked an agent to document an open mirrored database. It found the workspace, discovered the table schema, mapped the underlying files, and checked replication health—all from a single prompt.

That same scenario is now possible through the hosted OneLake MCP server. Once connected, ask:

“Document what’s in the House Price Open Mirror in my UK Property Data workspace.”

Figure: GitHub Copilot documents the House Price Open Mirror by using OneLake table and file tools.

The agent uses OneLake’s table and file tools to explore the database and build its response, working within your existing permissions. The experience is the same; there’s simply no local server to install or maintain.

The addition of the OneLake security tools extends what you can include in the documentation:

“Use the Fabric MCP server to document the OneLake security rules of the PricePaid table in the InlandRevenueHousePriceData mirror”

Figure: GitHub Copilot documents the OneLake security roles and permissions applied to the PricePaid table.

Querying OneLake

Agents need more than access to data—they need to know how best to query it. How do you turn a natural-language question into a query that works with data anywhere in OneLake? Continuing the house-price scenario, suppose you ask of the inland revenue database:

Question: “Using the InlandRevenue mirrored item from the TomDemo workspace, tell me how many houses were sold in Hampshire in 2020?”

Answer: “18,193 houses were sold in Hampshire in 2020, counting detached, semi-detached, and terraced houses. Including flats and maisonettes, the total was 21,452.”

How does the agent know how to answer this question just by asking OneLake? Endpoint discovery.

OneLake now provides an endpoint discovery API (Preview) that describes the Fabric Native engines available for each item and how to connect to them through skills, MCP servers, or engine-specific endpoints. The API also returns the OneLake Table APIs and File APIs so any agent can connect to the underlying data either directly or through tools like DuckDB.

When you include a simple instruction to use the discovery API and load the returned skill for the default engine, GitHub Copilot in VSCode turns a natural-language question into a query tailored to that engine.

Figure: GitHub Copilot in Visual Studio Code uses endpoint discovery to identify how to query the mirrored data.

To query data through OneLake, the data doesn’t have to live in OneLake. Shortcuts allow you to query data anywhere without making a copy. Shortcut transforms allow you to convert data files into tables without writing a single line of code to create or maintain the tables as the files change.

To continue the property price example, let’s combine the data from our mirrored database with some data in SharePoint. Mirrored databases are read-only, so here we’ll create a new Lakehouse to bring together our data and run a query:

“Please follow these steps using the Fabric and OneLake MCP tools:

  1. Using my existing SharePoint connection, you’ll find a folder in my OneDrive https://onedrive.cloud.microsoft/xxx/Documents/SampleData/council-tax-2026-27 that contains CSV data, can you create a new Lakehouse in the TomDemo workspace with a shortcut to this CSV, please use a shortcut transform to turn this CSV into a table.
  2. Create another shortcut to the Inland Revenue PricePaid table.
  3. Answer this question: What is the most expensive tax Band D, where is it, and how many homes were sold each year since 2000 in those postcodes?”

Answer: “Dorset has the highest 2026–27 Band D charge in the dataset: £2,765.02 annually, shared across 13,275 postcodes.”

Below is the Lakehouse that was built containing a delta table of our CSV data and the result of the query:

Figure: Lakehouse containing shortcuts to the council tax data and the Inland Revenue PricePaid table.Figure: GitHub Copilot returns annual home sales for the postcodes with the highest Band D council tax charge.

Because this is a Lakehouse, it exposes a Spark endpoint, which allows us to run an analysis to check if there is any correlation between the median house price of an area and its council tax band. GitHub Copilot picks the Spark CLI skill returned by the discovery API to perform this analysis:

Question: “now use the spark endpoint to run a spark job to see if median house price is correlated to the council tax band of the area - e.g., do higher tax bands have more expensive houses. Start with a Pearson correlation.”

Answer: “The Spark job found a negative Pearson correlation: r = −0.562. Councils with higher Band D charges tended to have lower, not higher, median house sale prices.”

Figure: GitHub Copilot uses the Spark CLI skill to run a Pearson correlation analysis in the Lakehouse.Figure: The analysis shows a negative correlation between Band D council tax charges and median house sale prices.

Now, all that’s left to do is check the results!

OneLake brings your data together; these new capabilities help agents put it to work. Combine catalog search in the Fabric Core MCP server with endpoint discovery and the returned skills, and an agent can find the data, connect to the right engine, and answer your question, all from a single prompt.

What skills will you build to bring these capabilities together, and what would you like us to add to Fabric? Try these tools with your own data and share what works and what’s missing. Your feedback will help shape what we build next.

fabric_blog:6eafeb6028b4.title: Modernize data integration strategy with Microsoft Fabric when using Snowflake and Databricks
fabric_blog:6eafeb6028b4.excerpt:
Challenges solved by Microsoft Fabric

Microsoft Fabric is an end-to-end analytics platform that brings together data integration, data engineering, warehousing, real-time analytics, business intelligence, and AI-related experiences. It has grown tremendously within the community because it is solving a key problem: lowering the integration tax across data and analytics systems. To understand the integration tax, consider a mid-sized or large organization that wants to perform analytics and data processing. It may use several source systems, an analytics platform such as a warehouse or lakehouse, and yet another platform or vendor for orchestration. To generate insights, the organization must integrate these different systems (hence the term integration tax).

Fabric brings together a broad set of analytics capabilities within one platform, which can reduce the number of separate integrations an organization needs to design and operate. You can bring data into Fabric, store it in a warehouse or lakehouse, query and analyze it with Spark or T-SQL, visualize insights with Power BI, and support real-time scenarios with Real-Time Intelligence. Fabric also interoperates with platforms such as Snowflake and Databricks, helping organizations unify data and analytics across technologies while minimizing data movement and duplication.

The following diagram shows how these experiences come together as part of the Microsoft Fabric platform.

Figure: Microsoft Fabric brings data, analytics, AI, OneLake, and governance capabilities together on a unified platform.

OneLake serves as Fabric's unified logical data layer. Fabric-managed data resides in OneLake, while shortcuts and some mirroring scenarios can reference data that remains outside OneLake. If one team owns the data and another team in the organization needs access, the second team does not need to duplicate it. Instead, it can create a Fabric shortcut and work with the same copy of the data.

Beyond storage, OneLake also enables data-sharing and governance patterns across domains and workspaces. Organizations can expose data through shortcuts while maintaining ownership within the producing team, enabling data mesh architecture without duplicating datasets.

Integration options

We have discussed shortcuts briefly. Now let's look at how they work and at the other options available for making data accessible in Fabric:

  • Shortcuts: Fabric lets you create a pointer to data in its existing location and access it without moving it. A shortcut is similar to a symbolic link or a Windows shortcut: the data source can differ from the location where users access it. For example, data can remain in Amazon S3 while a Fabric shortcut provides access to the required data. To users, the data appears to reside in Fabric even though it is retrieved from S3. Shortcut transformations also support selected transformations on shortcut data.
  • Mirroring: For supported data sources, mirroring provides you with a low latency option to bring your data into Fabric. Depending on the source system, mirroring either continuously replicates data into OneLake or exposes the source through metadata mirroring and shortcuts. This approach reduces the need to manage pipelines or infrastructure and can offload analytical workloads from the source system. For example, if source data resides in an on-premises SQL Server database, you can create a SQL Server mirror in Fabric and analyze the latest available data there.
  • Open Mirroring: This is an extension of mirroring for any data sources that are specific to your organization. Open Mirroring enables applications or partners to write changes directly into an open mirroring landing zone, after which Fabric converts and manages the data as Delta tables.
  • Pipelines: are an option when a solution requires explicit data movement, multi-step orchestration, complex transformations, or integration across multiple sources.

The following diagram illustrates how mirroring and shortcuts complement Fabric compute experiences by either bringing data into Fabric or making externally stored data available without traditional ingestion.

Figure: Mirroring and shortcuts provide different approaches for making source data available to Fabric workloads.

User layer: AI Foundry and Copilot Studio with data agents

Making enterprise data accessible in Fabric is only the first step. Once that data is available through a governed integration pattern, organizations can build AI experiences that allow users and applications to interact with it using natural language.

Microsoft Fabric Data Agents allow users to interact with governed data using natural language and can generate and execute queries across supported Fabric experiences. Data Agents make it possible to gain insights directly from data without building an agent from scratch.

After creating a Data Agent, you can publish it to applications or other consumer experiences. As shown in the AI Agent Decision Tree, several consumer-layer options are available. This article focuses on two: Copilot Studio and Microsoft AI Foundry.

Copilot Studio

Copilot Studio is a low-code platform for building agents that combine generative AI with enterprise data and system actions. It is a practical option for employee or customer self-service, support automation, conversational access to Fabric data, and workflows where an agent needs to retrieve information or invoke an existing business process.

After publishing a Fabric Data Agent, you can connect it to Copilot Studio to build a custom agent that also uses other data sources. You can then publish the agent to Microsoft 365 experiences such as Teams. This option works well for common, out-of-the-box scenarios that a large language model can support without extensive customization.

Microsoft AI Foundry

Microsoft AI Foundry is where you would go when you need more control over how an AI application or agent is built and operated. It brings models, agents, tools, evaluation, and monitoring into one place, while still letting developers choose how much code and customization they want. In the context of Fabric, a Foundry agent can use a Fabric data agent as one of its tools, so it can work with governed enterprise data alongside other knowledge sources and business systems.

This option is well suited to use cases that require greater control over model behavior, orchestration, evaluation, and customization. Microsoft AI Foundry is typically best suited for professional developer scenarios.

Next steps

Microsoft Fabric provides multiple approaches for connecting existing data estates to analytics and AI workloads. Start by identifying whether your scenario requires data replication, virtualization, or explicit data movement, and then use the decision guide to choose the appropriate starting point.

To explore these capabilities in more detail:

  • Learn how OneLake shortcuts make external data available to Fabric without traditional data movement.
  • Explore Mirroring in Microsoft Fabric for supported databases and data platforms.
  • Learn how Microsoft Fabric Data Factory pipelines support orchestration and data movement.
  • Explore Fabric data agents for natural-language interaction with governed Fabric data.
  • Learn how to connect a Fabric data agent to Copilot Studio or Microsoft AI Foundry.

simon_willison:9b0f1b3870f8.title: Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too
simon_willison:9b0f1b3870f8.excerpt:
Yesterday's hot paper was Sparks of Weight-Space Programming: LLMs can natively read & write neural network weights by Rikiya Takehi, Jayden Teoh, Alex Zhang, and Omar Khattab. The paper (OK, the authors classify is as a "blog post", but it's paper-shaped) found that frontier models, in particular GPT-6 Astra, can both interpret and modify the raw weights of a machine learning model - literally a text description of the model containing a bunch of floating point numbers. I've been playing with one of the examples from the paper and I'm delighted to share that Qwen 3.8 27B running on my laptop can do this as well!

Weight-Space Programming

Here's the highlight from their abstract, describing impressive capabilities for GPT-6 Astra and coining the term Weight-Space Programming for when LLMs analyze and modify model weights:

Just by looking at the raw weights, GPT-6 Astra can tell what a network was trained to do. And without any environment feedback, it has no trouble writing, from scratch, small game-playing networks that outplay networks trained with PPO for 100 million steps.

Likewise, asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, Astra identifies an issue in its weights causing reasoning loops that Qwen’s own model card warns about, and fixes this by natively editing 0.016% of the weights. With the same sampling settings, this weight correction raises MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% and generalizes out of the box to instruction following, raising IFEval by 3x.

All of this is possible without allowing Astra to write training loops. It uses its reasoning to figure out what each part of a neural network computes, or should compute, and changes the weights accordingly. We call this Weight-Space Programming.

The paper combines two topics that I think deserve to be treated separately. The first is what models can do with raw weights without running tools or executing code. The second explores how well models, once armed with code, can run operations to update and improve other models.

spaCy author Matthew Honnibal called the paper misleading for conflating the two, and Sean Goedecke deconstructed the Qwen3.5-0.8B update example as taking the same steps that a human ML researcher would use.

I'm going to focus on the no-tools question, which I think is the more interesting of the two.

The paper presents the first question as Can LLMs understand model behaviors from weights? They trained four neural networks to play simplified 10x10 grid versions of four classic computer games - Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, and Freeway (I had to look that one up, it's an Atari 2600 game from 1981). Then they fed those weights (as floating point numbers) to an LLM along with the following question:

The weights below belong to one policy network that was trained with reinforcement learning to play a game on this grid. Which game was it trained on? Work from the weights. You have no tools: no code execution, no calculator, nothing to run. This is a single response.

The GitHub repository that accompanies the paper is RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs. The exp1_which_game folder contains the prompts they used, with weights for the four games:

  • breakout/prompt.txt
  • freeway/prompt.txt
  • pacman/prompt.txt
  • pong/prompt.txt

I checked and, aside from the weights, each prompt is identical to the others.

Trying it out with Qwen 3.8 27B and other models

The prompts on GitHub are self-contained. My LLM tool has a -f/--fragment option which can be passed the URL to a text file to use as a prompt, which means I can run any of the above like this:

llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/breakout/prompt.txt \
  -m openrouter/moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro

This example requires the llm-openrouter plugin installed, and runs the Breakout prompt against Kimi K3.1 Pro via OpenRouter. Here's what I got back from Kimi K3.1 Pro, which successfully guessed Breakout after 9m 41s and 19,493 reasoning tokens.

But how about Qwen 3.8 27B? That's still my favorite model to run on my own laptop - it's just 17GB (I use this version) and somehow feels close to the leading proprietary models of 2025.

I fired up LM Studio, ensured Qwen 3.8 27B was loaded with a long context window (the default 8192 context failed with errors), installed the llm-lmstudio plugin and ran this command:

LMSTUDIO_TIMEOUT=900 \
  llm -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/RikiyaT/lm_understand-logs/refs/heads/main/exp1_which_game/runs/pacman/prompt.txt \
  -m lmstudio/qwen/qwen3.8-27b

(I had to bump the timeout up using an environment variable, see this issue.)

After 46m 12s and 43,506 reasoning tokens, Qwen on my laptop returned a response that ended like this (here's the reasoning trace):

Game: A simplified Pac-Man-style gridworld: an agent moves through a fixed 8x8 maze with central and corner wall blocks, moving objects/ghosts, and reward targets/pellets.

Description: The agent navigates a fixed maze-like 8x8 board, using current agent/moving-object/previous-frame cues to move through corridors, collect reward-target cells, and avoid moving objects or hazards.

Confidence: 72%

This is impressive. I tried it on two of the other games as well. It identified Pong (reasoning) in 1h 4m 54s:

Pong — specifically a Pong-like paddle/ball game where the agent controls a vertical paddle on the right side and must move up/down to intercept or return a moving ball/reward object.

Description:

The agent moves a right-side paddle vertically to hit or catch a moving ball-like reward target moving across the 8×8 field, while a left-side moving object/opponent and wall borders define the play; reward is obtained by successfully intercepting/returning/scoring the ball, and missing or failing to hit it is penalized.

Confidence:

75%

And Breakout (reasoning) in 52m 25s:

Game: Breakout, or an Arkanoid-like paddle/ball/brick game.

Description: The agent is a paddle on the bottom row and moves left/right to keep a ball in play; the ball moves around the upper grid, and bricks/reward targets in the top rows give reward when hit, while missing the ball/hitting the bottom wall ends the episode or gives penalty.

Confidence: 88%

Qwen failed at the Freeway prompt, which didn't surprise me considering that game is more obscure than the other three. Here's that transcript - Qwen thought it was "A simplified Pac-Man-like grid game: agent moves 4-directionally".

The reasoning traces are fun to skim, and almost incomprehensible. Here's a sample:

What about agent channel0? We see some large channel0 rows near row8 col7/8 and maybe bottom? Let's list channel0 large: line436 input435 (row8 col7 ch0) -2.107,1.169,0.513...; line441 input440 (row8 col8 ch0) -0.376,0.010,1.564,3.855...; line445 input444 (row8 col8 ch4) 0.142,0.491...; line382? input381 ch0? Wait line382 input381: 381//5=76 (row7 col6), ch1? 381%5=1? 76 * 5=380, ch1. So not. Channel0 large maybe at row8 col7/8 only. Also top row? line44 input43 ch3, line49 ch3. Channel0 large maybe not many. Agent position could be near bottom-right? If the agent is typically at bottom-right?

That said though, I expect a sufficiently experienced human being armed with a notepad and a pencil could get there with enough effort.

It's a cool paper, but some of the wider commentary I've seen around it does not feel justified. I'm not ready to declare that the age of source code is over and our future involves incomprehensible machines editing their own model weights in incomprehensible ways.

You are only seeing the long-form articles from my blog. Subscribe to /atom/everything/ to get all of my posts, or take a look at my other subscription options.

dbt-core 1.13.0-rc1 - November 04, 2026

Breaking Changes

  • Drop support for Python 3.10, which has reached end-of-life (#TBD)

Fixes

  • Recognize Databricks Python model config keys (access_control_list, notebook_access_control_list) in jsonschema validation so they no longer raise spurious CustomKeyInConfigDeprecation warnings (dbt-databricks#1661) (#N/A)
  • Macro namespace resolution no longer lets an internal search_package shadow adapter or root overrides. When search_package is itself an internal package (e.g. dbt or dbt_postgres), the adapter override is now consistently preferred over the base dbt implementation, and a root-project macro always wins. (#16540)
  • Accept the dbt v2-only info_schema, check-paths and checks keys in dbt_project.yml, ignoring them with a note that they are specific to the dbt v2 engine (#16640)

fabric_blog:eb6fb91698c7.title: Find expensive queries from Capacity Metrics (Generally Available)
fabric_blog:eb6fb91698c7.excerpt:
When warehouse capacity usage spikes, you need to quickly understand what ran, which warehouse drove the usage, and which queries require investigation. 

The Monitor in warehouse action in the Microsoft Fabric Capacity Metrics app connects the capacity-level view directly to Warehouse Monitor. It opens the selected warehouse with the relevant time window already applied, eliminating manual correlation across monitoring experiences. 

Figure: Animated GIF - demonstrating how to navigate from a Capacity Metrics timepoint to Warehouse Monitor in four steps.

Follow the activity into your warehouse 

  1. Open Capacity Metrics: From the Compute page, select your capacity and review CU % over time. Capacity Units, or CUs, represent the compute consumption tracked for the capacity.
  2. Choose a timepoint: Select the usage increase you want to investigate, and then select Explore and open TimePoint Detail.
  3. Choose an operation window: Under Background operations for time range, select a supported warehouse query operation whose Start and End times cover the interval. Then select Monitor in warehouse.
  4. Explore Warehouse Monitor: Open Query history to review statements that ran during the selected interval. 

Access required: Access to the Capacity Metrics app and the Admin role in the workspace containing the warehouse. For supported operations and navigation, refer to the Monitor in warehouse documentation.

Find the queries worth investigating 

Start with CPU time. Add the column through Column options and sort from highest to lowest. CPU time is the processor time allocated to an execution. It is not elapsed duration or the Capacity Units billed for an individual query. 

No single metric explains the complete workload. Review these columns together: 

  • Data scanned: Identify statements that read large volumes of data. Compare OneLake reads with local disk, and memory reads to understand caching behavior. 
  • Result cache hit: A value of 2 means the query reused a cached result, 1 means the execution created a result set cache, and 0 means result caching did not apply. 
  • Query text: Review joins, predicates, and filters for unnecessary scans or processing. 
  • Label: Connect statements to a workload, business process, or test variation. 
  • Is distributed: Separate distributed executions, represented by 1, from nondistributed requests, represented by 0. 

For queries with high CPU time or data scanned, select View similar runs to determine whether the behavior is recurring or isolated. Add Query Insights fields such as application, SQL pool, status, and error code to identify the originating workload and distinguish expensive successful executions from failed or interrupted ones. 

For field definitions, refer to the query execution history column reference documentation.

Make the same correlation with AI 

The Data Warehouse operations skill in Skills for Fabric can correlate Capacity Metrics data with Query Insights activity for the same warehouse and time window, using your existing permissions. 

Example prompt: 

Investigate the capacity spike for my warehouse from 14:00 to 15:00 UTC on November 3, 2026. Identify queries with high CPU time or data scanned, explain why each query stands out, and suggest the next investigation step. 

Review the supporting metrics and query details before making tuning or workload-management decisions. 

Next steps 

Try Monitor in warehouse the next time you see a capacity usage increase. Start with CPU time and data scanned, compare similar runs, and use workload metadata to determine what drove the activity. 

For more guidance, refer to the Warehouse performance guidelines, query blocking troubleshooting, and Monitor T-SQL queries documentation.

fabric_blog:3cf817db3b41.title: OneLake table APIs: Now with Iceberg writes, plus richer table metadata (Preview)
fabric_blog:3cf817db3b41.excerpt:
OneLake table APIs already let Iceberg-compatible engines discover and read tables in Microsoft Fabric. Today we're taking the next step with two additions: Iceberg REST Catalog (IRC) writes through the OneLake table endpoint, now available, and a new additional table metadata API, in preview, for adding descriptions and tags to tables and columns. Together, they make OneLake a place where any engine can not only read data, but also publish it, with the business context people and AI agents need to use it well. 

Write native Iceberg tables from the engines you already use

Until now, the OneLake Iceberg endpoint supported read-only metadata operations. Now, IRC-compatible clients can create native Iceberg tables, commit new snapshots, and request short-lived storage credentials through the same endpoint they already use for reads. That means engines such as PyIceberg, Snowflake, and DuckDB can land results directly in OneLake using standard Iceberg tooling, with no custom connectors or copy jobs.

Some of the supported Iceberg REST Catalog operations at the OneLake table endpoint include: 

Operation 

What it does 

Status 

List/get/check namespaces 

Discovers the schemas in a data item 

Available 

List/get/check tables 

Discovers tables and returns their Iceberg metadata 

Available 

Create table 

Creates a native Iceberg table in a schema 

New! 

Commit table updates 

Commits new snapshots and metadata changes to a native Iceberg table 

New! 

Drop table 

Removes a table and its data from OneLake 

New! 

Load table credentials 

Returns short-lived storage credentials for a table (credential vending) 

New! 

Writes are built for multi-engine environments. Commits use optimistic concurrency checks, so a conflicting update fails instead of silently overwriting a newer table state. Credential vending lets clients write data files without managing separate storage access. And because the tables live in OneLake, they're immediately discoverable by every tool connected to the catalog.  

Many industry partners are already building on this feature. Snowflake supports the OneLake table APIs through the catalog-linked database feature, which automatically discovers schemas and tables in a Fabric data item, so Snowflake users can read, create, and write Iceberg tables in OneLake. ClickHouse also announced that it now writes Iceberg tables directly to OneLake using these APIs. 

Add business context to tables and columns 

Data is only as useful as people's understanding of it. The new additional table metadata API (preview) lets you read and write descriptions and key-value tags for a table and its columns, for example to explain a table's business purpose, record its owning team, or describe how to interpret a column. It uses one common REST route, so you don't need a format-specific catalog API to do it. 

It also works through internal OneLake shortcuts: updates apply to the target table, so everyone sees the same context whether they read through the shortcut or the source. 

Explore more in the OneLake documentation 

Check out our documentation for more information. This includes end-to-end samples, from configuring PyIceberg, Snowflake, and DuckDB for writes and credential vending to a Python sample that updates table metadata safely. Start with the following resources: 

  • OneLake table APIs overview
  • OneLake Iceberg metadata API
  • Iceberg table API samples
  • Read and write additional table metadata (preview) 

We want your feedback! 

Start writing Iceberg tables to OneLake and try the additional table metadata preview today and share your experience with us. 

Have feedback? Share your ideas and vote at the Fabric Ideas site and join the conversation in the Microsoft Fabric Community.

fabric_blog:2fe4fbe32c22.title: Govern Fabric connections with admin APIs and data connection policies (Preview)
fabric_blog:2fe4fbe32c22.excerpt:
Co-author: Abhishek Narain

Protect continuity, understand connection risk, and set tenant-wide guardrails 

Imagine that the person who built a business-critical pipeline has left your organization. The connection still exists, but nobody is sure who can manage it or whether its credentials will keep working. What begins as a handover problem quickly becomes a governance question: who owns your connections, where do they lead, and which identities should be allowed to use them? 

Microsoft Fabric brings these questions together through two complementary capabilities:

  • Admin connection APIs give tenant administrators visibility and ownership-management tools across connection types.  
  • Data connection policies set preventive controls for cloud connections.  

Together, they support a practical sequence: restore responsibility, understand your connections, then enforce the authentication boundaries your organization needs. 

From recovery to prevention

Keep work moving when a connection owner leaves 

A departure should not leave a connection without someone who can maintain it. When an existing connection has a single owner, a Fabric tenant administrator can use the admin connection APIs to grant the Owner role to a responsible successor, another administrator, or an appropriate service principal. This restores the ability to manage the connection and establishes clear accountability during the handover. 

Use the admin connection APIs to review current access, assign a responsible successor as an Owner, update an existing assignment, and remove access that is no longer appropriate. The role-assignment endpoints support GET, POST, PATCH, and DELETE operations; refer to Admin Connections REST API reference for endpoint syntax and examples.

Ownership is only part of continuity. Granting Owner does not transfer or renew OAuth credentials, confer permissions on the source system, or guarantee that dependent workloads will run. The incoming owner must check the connection requirements, update or reauthenticate credentials where needed, and validate the workloads that depend on it. Treat that validation as part of offboarding, not a task to postpone until something fails. 

See your connections, endpoints, and access clearly 

A tenant-wide inventory helps administrators find ownership gaps, unexpected access, and connections that may require review before they become operational issues. The admin APIs provide visibility across all connection types, including connections you do not own or have permission to manage. By comparison, the standard Manage connections and gateways experience does not provide a tenant-wide inventory, even for administrators. 

Use the tenant-wide connections endpoint to collect the complete inventory, including all paginated results. The response includes connection names and IDs, connectivity and connector types, endpoint paths, privacy levels, and credential or authentication-type metadata—but not secret values. Combine this information with current role assignments to identify unexpected access and endpoints or domains that require closer review. 

Recency data can help prioritize the review. Created, last-linked, and last-credentials-used timestamps answer different questions: last linked indicates when the connection configuration was most recently associated with a workload, while last credentials used provides a runtime signal. These timestamps do not provide a complete historical audit log, an automatic dependency map, or proof that an apparently idle connection is safe to delete. Confirm critical dependencies with workload owners before making changes. 

Figure: Animated GIF — Read-only Fabric Connection Inventory sample app showing illustrative data; no live tenant details or ownership changes are shown.

This read-only demonstration uses a Python client to list tenant connections and inspect a connection role assignment. It does not change ownership. For the admin API endpoints and an example response, refer to List Connections (Admin) and List Connection Role Assignments (Admin). 

Try a read-only connection inventory app 

For a hands-on inventory, refer to the Fabric Connection Inventory sample app. It uses the admin connection APIs to list tenant connections and their Owner and PendingOwner assignments, with search and filters for reviewing connector types, endpoints, and ownership results. It does not change connections, assign owners, or enforce policies. 

This is a single-tenant deployment template, not a hosted app that readers can sign into. To use it, an organization must deploy its own instance in a workspace that supports Fabric Apps (Preview), configure a single-tenant Microsoft Entra app, grant delegated Tenant.Read.All consent, and sign in with a Fabric administrator account. See the repository’s setup instructions. 

Illustrative API examples 

To inventory connections across the tenant, an administrator can make a read-only request: 

GET https://api.fabric.microsoft.com/v1/admin/connections 
Authorization: Bearer <access-token> 

{ 
  "value": [ 
    { 
      "id": "11111111-1111-4111-8111-111111111111", 
      "displayName": "ContosoConnection", 
      "connectivityType": "ShareableCloud", 
      "connectionDetails": { 
        "type": "Web", 
        "path": "https://www.contoso.com/"
      } 
    } 
  ] 
} 

If the response includes a continuationToken, use it to request the next page. 

For an ownership handoff, the following illustrative write request shows the payload for adding a user as an Owner. It was not part of the read-only GIF or the production test: 

POST https://api.fabric.microsoft.com/v1/admin/connections/11111111-1111-4111-8111-111111111111/roleAssignments 
Authorization: Bearer <access-token> 
Content-Type: application/json 
 
{ 
  "principal": { 
    "id": "22222222-2222-4222-8222-222222222222", 
    "type": "User" 
  }, 
  "role": "Owner" 
} 

An ownership assignment may require the incoming owner to reauthenticate. It does not transfer credentials or guarantee that dependent workloads will run. 

Make approved authentication methods the rule 

An inventory shows how connections authenticate today. An authentication allowlist turns your organization’s requirements into a tenant-wide boundary for cloud connections. Instead of relying on every creator to make the same choice, you define the methods that policy permits. 

An authentication allowlist helps administrators reduce inconsistent or noncompliant authentication choices across cloud connections. In the Fabric admin portal, select Data Policies in the left navigation, then open the Authentication allowlist tab. Add the approved authentication methods, turn on Restrict to allowlist, and select Save. Review the tenant-wide confirmation before committing. Select methods that meet your organization’s requirements and are supported by the relevant connectors; no single method is universally available or appropriate. 

When enforcement is enabled, methods outside the allowlist fail policy evaluation for existing as well as new cloud connections. Enable this carefully, because it can disrupt existing workflows. That makes the inventory essential preparation: identify affected connections, agree on supported alternatives with their owners, and plan credential changes before enabling the restriction. These controls govern cloud connections; they are not a promise of coverage for every gateway, desktop client, or data path. 

Figure: Authentication allowlist example before enforcement. Restrict to allowlist is turned off, and Workspace identity is included as a sample entry.

Define which Microsoft Entra tenants can authenticate connections 

An approved authentication method does not make every Microsoft Entra tenant acceptable. Organizations may also need to block connection authentication associated with unapproved tenants. The Tenant allowlist addresses this requirement by defining which Microsoft Entra tenants can be used for Entra-authenticated cloud connections, helping reduce the risk of authentication through unapproved tenant identities. 

On Tenant allowlist, select Add tenant ID and enter the approved tenant GUIDs. Validate each ID carefully: the experience does not look up friendly names, and the list supports up to 100 IDs. Turn on Restrict to allowlist, select Save, and review the tenant-wide confirmation. Once enforced, the restriction affects both existing and new Entra-authenticated cloud connections. 

Keep identity and destination controls distinct. The Authentication allowlist limits which methods cloud connections can use, while the Tenant allowlist limits which Microsoft Entra tenants they can authenticate with. Neither control approves destination endpoints nor acts as a firewall rule. 

Figure: Tenant allowlist example before enforcement: Restrict to allowlist is off. The GUID shown is fictitious.

Start with visibility, then enforce 

Before enabling enforcement, inventory your cloud connections, identify critical workloads and their owners, and confirm the authentication methods and Microsoft Entra tenant IDs they need. Review the Authentication allowlist and Tenant allowlist tabs together, then enable only the controls you intend to enforce. Each allowlist has its own Restrict to allowlist switch. Communicate the change and assess its effect on existing as well as new cloud connections; enforcement applies tenant-wide. 

Policy changes can take up to one hour to take effect. After enforcement begins, test affected cloud connections and dependent workloads. A noncompliant new connection is rejected; an existing connection may show Policy Evaluation Failure and go Offline. Open the connection details to identify the cause, then work with the connection owner and tenant admin to resolve the authentication-method or tenant-policy mismatch. Ownership transfer alone does not resolve a policy failure. 

Figure: Connection details explain a policy failure. In this example, OAuth 2.0 non-Entra ID is not an allowed authentication kind.

Closing 

Start with a complete inventory and an ownership review of critical connections. Use that evidence to define and validate authentication-method and Microsoft Entra tenant allowlists. These capabilities cannot prevent every outage or misuse, but they can reduce unmanaged handovers, clarify decisions about access and endpoints, and apply preventive controls that reflect your organization’s requirements. 

To plan your implementation, review the guidance for data source management and data connection policies.

fabric_blog:fdd5d7528171.title: Bring your Fabric data into your next app with connectors
fabric_blog:fdd5d7528171.excerpt:
Most business applications start with data that already exists. Customer orders may live in a Fabric SQL database. Inventory history may be in a Lakehouse. Sales performance may already be modeled in Power BI. The opportunity is not to move that data again, but to turn trusted data into an experience that helps people make decisions and take action.  

Connectors in Fabric Apps shorten that path. They give an app a consistent way to work with Fabric data, so developers can spend less time on integration plumbing and more time building the experience users need.  

Connect to the Fabric data you already trust. Build the experience your users need. Keep the application close to the data and governance foundation already in place.  

Instead of beginning with infrastructure, start with the customer's need: What should this app help someone understand, decide, or do?  

From data to an application  

Imagine a large telecommunications provider operating thousands of cell sites and serving millions of customers. Network telemetry may stream into a Lakehouse; service-impact and incident data may live in a Fabric SQL database; and trusted availability and capacity measures may already be modeled in Power BI.  

A report can show where the service is degrading. But a network operations engineer may need to go further:  

  • Which sites and customers are affected?  
  • Is the issue driven by congestion, equipment, power, or an upstream dependency?  
  • What maintenance work or recent changes are associated with the site?  
  • Can I create or update an incident and route the next action from the same experience?  

This is where a Fabric App adds value. Connectors let the app combine governed network and operational data in one task-oriented experience for investigation, triage, and action.  

Architecture: Network operations app  

Figure: Fabric data remains the foundation; connectors bring network and operational context into a task-oriented Fabric App.

Network telemetry remains in Fabric; operational records stay in their governed source; and trusted measures continue to come from the semantic model. The Fabric App brings those sources together so an engineer can move from a network signal to an informed operational action without reconstructing context across multiple tools. 

Choose the connector that matches the job  

Choose the connector that matches the Fabric item and the job the app needs to perform. Fabric Apps supports documented connector patterns for lakehouse SQL analytics endpoints, warehouses, SQL databases in Fabric, and Power BI semantic models.  

Fabric source  

Connector type  

Documented operations  

Lakehouse SQL analytics endpoint  

fabric-sqlanalytics  

Read  

Warehouse  

fabric-warehouse  

Read, create, update, delete  

SQL database in Fabric  

fabric-sqldatabase  

Read, create, update, delete  

Power BI semantic model  

fabric-semanticmodel  

executeQuery  

Request only the operations the scenario needs. For example, a read-only inventory experience should not request write access. An operational app that updates a warehouse or SQL database should make that requirement explicit.  

Three real-world patterns 

Incident triage 

A telecommunications provider can build a network operations app on a Lakehouse, Fabric SQL database, and semantic model. An engineer can search for a cell site; review latency, congestion, availability, and impacted services; inspect recent maintenance or configuration changes; and create or update the operational incident from one experience.  

Value: The engineer moves from detecting service degradation to understanding impact and coordinating the next action without switching across disconnected monitoring and case-management views. 

Customer 360 for sellers 

A sales team may have accounts and order data in a warehouse, product signals in a Lakehouse, and trusted revenue measures in a semantic model. A Fabric App can organize this information around the account and add a tailored experience for exploration, notes, recommended next steps, or AI-assisted questions.  

Value: The app is designed around the seller’s job, not around the boundaries between data systems. 

Retail store operations from a semantic model 

Imagine a retailer such as Nordstrom with trusted sales, inventory, fulfillment, and customer-service measures already defined in a Power BI semantic model. A Fabric App can use that model as the analytical foundation for a store operations experience where a manager reviews daily performance, identifies products at risk of stocking out, investigates order or pickup delays, and coordinates the next action with the store team.  

Value: Store teams reuse trusted business measures and move from insight to action without recreating logic or switching across multiple reports and operational tools.  

Start with one focused workflow  

A good first app starts with a narrow, valuable job. The builder journey is:  

  1. Create or initialize a Fabric Apps project.  
  2. Identify the Fabric item behind the workflow.  
  3. Add a connector with only the operations the app needs.  
  4. Test with the permissions and data boundaries expected for users.  

For example, a read-only warehouse connection can expose governed site and service-impact data to the app:  

npx rayfin connector add \  
  --type fabric-warehouse \  
  --workspace-id YOUR_WORKSPACE_ID \  
  --item-id YOUR_WAREHOUSE_ITEM_ID \  
  --name network-operations \  
  --operations read 

The connector is added to the project configuration and can then be used through the generated connector interface. For complete syntax, supported operations, prerequisites, and current limitations, see Connect Fabric Apps to Fabric data.  

Build from the data you already trust  

Your most valuable business data is already in Microsoft Fabric. Connectors help you turn that data into focused applications that do more than display insight by helping you complete real business tasks. Get started with Fabric App and connect to your data.

fabric_blog:a72fbd9496d2.title: Salesforce Data 360 integration with OneLake (Preview)
fabric_blog:a72fbd9496d2.excerpt:
A customer reports a missing delivery. The service case is in Salesforce, while the shipping and returns records are in Microsoft Fabric. Before a team can decide what to do next, it needs to connect those two views of the same customer experience.

For many organizations, answering questions like this still means exporting customer data, building ingestion pipelines, and maintaining another copy for analytics. Every additional handoff adds work for data teams and another dataset to secure and reconcile. Business teams wait for a complete picture while customer decisions move ahead. 

Zero-copy file sharing offers a different approach by making source data available where it is needed for analysis, without first building a separate ingestion copy. The data is always current. This makes it easier to connect customer context with the financial, operational, and product information that gives it meaning. 

Introducing Salesforce Data 360 integration with OneLake 

Salesforce Data 360 Integration with OneLake is now available in preview. Using OneLake Shortcuts, organizations can make Salesforce Data 360 data available in a Fabric and query them alongside enterprise data. Salesforce Data 360 remains the source, while Microsoft OneLake brings the analysis together. 

Those shortcuts reference the data in Salesforce Data 360 rather than importing a separate copy into the lakehouse. Further, the data is always current without requiring you to do any additional refresh. Teams can use the lakehouse, warehouse, and other Fabric Engines to explore customer data, join it with other enterprise tables, and develop analytics using familiar Fabric experiences, including SQL and Spark. Key benefits include: 

  • Less integration work. Reference shared Salesforce data without building and maintaining a separate ingestion pipeline just to make it available in Fabric. 
  • More complete business insight in real time. Bring customer cases, accounts, and opportunities represented in shared Data Lake Objects into analysis with orders, financial transactions, and operational records in real time. As data is available in Data 360, it is immediately available in OneLake. 

Once you have the data in OneLake, you can target the following use cases: 

  • Customer retention analysis using Spark. Use Fabric notebooks to prepare features from shared customer data and operational history for churn or propensity models, subject to the organization's data-use and access policies. 
  • Customer profitability Dashboards. Combine shared customer and account Data Lake Objects with financial data in OneLake to examine revenue, service costs, and margin together. Build Power BI reporting on an appropriately configured semantic model. 
  • Churn Prediction. OneLake is integrated with Microsoft Foundry. Salesforce Data 360 data can be used with Microsoft Foundry to build ML models to predict churn. 
  • Ask questions about your data. Build Ontologies with Salesforce Data 360 and ask questions using Data Agents that will respond to context established with Ontologies. 

Getting started 

Prerequisites 

You need Salesforce Data 360 access with the Data Cloud Architect permission set and an edition that supports data sharing. Identify the Data Lake Objects to share and prepare a Fabric workspace with a lakehouse and permission to create table shortcuts. 

Decide on an authentication method supported by the connection: Use organizational account for testing and prototyping. Use Service principal method for production applications. If you use a service principal, register the application in Microsoft Entra ID and prepare the required credential. 

Configure Salesforce Data 360 shortcuts 

Prepare the Salesforce share in Salesforce Data 360: Create a data share containing the required Data Lake Objects. Create a Microsoft OneLake data share target using the Microsoft Entra tenant ID and the appropriate identity's object ID, then link the share to that target. 

Figure: Creating a data share in Salesforce Data 360

Create a Shortcut in Fabric: In the destination lakehouse, select Get data > New table shortcut > Salesforce Data 360. Use the target's Tenant Endpoint as the Salesforce instance URL and its Core Tenant ID as the Salesforce org ID, then configure authentication. Choose the shared Data Lake Objects, save the shortcuts, and query a selected object. Confirm that the target is linked in Salesforce and test access with the intended Fabric users and workloads. 

Figure: Creating a Salesforce Data 360 shortcut using the share

During preview, only Data Lake Objects with the _dll extension is supported. Data Model Objects, Calculated Insight Objects, and schema-level shortcuts are not supported. 

We are excited to see what you build 

Salesforce Data 360 Integration with OneLake brings customer context closer to the enterprise data that helps teams act on it. By replacing a separate ingestion step with shared access through shortcuts, organizations can simplify the path from a business question to analysis while making access boundaries explicit. This integration advances the Microsoft Fabric and OneLake vision: make data easier to use together without requiring every source to move into one place. Salesforce Data 360 Shortcuts documentation provides you detailed information to get started.

Share your feedback and use cases in the Microsoft Fabric Community. Your experience will help shape what comes next as we continue connecting customer data with enterprise analytics.
