simon_whiteley:69e6ebb6e3d5.title: My Story Into Data: Aoife O'Kane Hackett
simon_whiteley:69e6ebb6e3d5.excerpt:
“When I started working in data, I couldn't have told you what a data engineer did. I was put on the team, and I ended up really, really liking it.”

There’s an assumption that people working in data and AI have always known exactly where they were going. That somewhere along the way there was a carefully thought-out career plan, a computer science degree and a straight line into technology. In fact, that’s not the case for many.

Aoife didn’t start out with a grand plan for where her career would take her. What she did have was curiosity, an openness to opportunities and a willingness to keep learning. One opportunity led to another and, somewhere along the way, she realised she had found a career she genuinely loved, one that brought together the things she was naturally good at with the things she found most interesting.

Growing up, she loved maths. At secondary school that became a love of physics, which eventually took her to university to study astrophysics. It was there, almost as part of something else, that she first encountered Python and began doing more substantial data analysis as part of her final-year project. She enjoyed it enough to start thinking that perhaps data could offer a route forward after university, although precisely what that career might look like was far from clear.

“I went from being really unsure of what to do after graduating to starting to look into some data graduate programmes.”

She was accepted onto a general data and AI graduate programme and placed into a data engineering team. And that's where the story takes a wonderfully honest turn.

“I probably couldn't have told you what a data engineer did before being put on that team. I was just put there, but then I ended up really, really liking it. It worked out for the best for me, and I've just grown from there.”

Finding the Thing That Fits

Four years into her career in data and engineering, the connection between the child who loved maths and consultant Aoife today makes much more sense. It is the problem solving that still gets her.

She enjoys taking a problem, understanding what is really being asked, evaluating the different options and eventually finding a way through it. Consulting adds another dimension because she gets to do that alongside people who bring different experience and knowledge to the problem, learning from them and then carrying those lessons into whatever comes next.

As she puts it, there is a “social element of the problem solving”, and the variety in consulting keeps the work interesting. Different businesses bring different requirements, different desired outcomes and different contexts, even when some of the underlying technology may be familiar.

Today her work includes building and maintaining client data platforms in Databricks and creating monitoring solutions around them, and she has worked across finance, healthcare and the charity sector. On one current project, for example, her team is developing a platform for a biotechnology company that moves data from testing machines back to laboratories, with a focus on getting that information there quickly while keeping it structured, correct and visible when issues arise.

“I am constantly learning, this is important to me. In data, its not about having all the answers, but about being curious enough to keep finding the next question”.

Seeing That It's Possible

When I ask Aoife whether she sees a noticeable gender gap in data, she doesn’t hesitate.

The teams she has worked with in consulting have been predominantly male and, at times, she has been one of only a few women on the team. She's also noticed the relative lack of women in data leadership.

“I think that it is quite clear to see the representation gap, I think we have quite a long way to go, but I can see positive change happening”.

Aoife remembers being actively encouraged at school to consider technical industries and recalls initiatives aimed at encouraging girls towards data and technology beginning to emerge. For her, part of changing participation is remarkably simple: young women need to be able to see that these careers exist for them.

“It's kind of just seeing that it's possible and being told you can do it.”

It's a short observation, but perhaps one of the most important in her story. Getting women into data is only one part of changing the balance. What happens when they arrive matters too.

The Difference One Person Can Make

When Aoife joined Advancing Analytics, she had a female manager for the first time and admits that she hadn't anticipated how much of a difference that would make.

Her manager at the time became someone she could watch progress through the organisation to principal level, but it wasn't simply career progression that made an impression. Aoife talks openly about the encouragement she has had to speak up, give opinions, give and accept feedback which has consistently supported developing confidence in herself.

“I didn't really anticipate how much of a difference in having such a great female mentor would make - having someone to ensure you were happy, comfortable, and confident contributing to discussions enabled me to have confidence in myself.”

It is an interesting lesson in what inclusion can look like in practice. Sometimes it isn't a programme or a policy. Sometimes it is having someone notice, ask the question, listen and make sure your voice is in the room.

And that's something Aoife recognises in the wider culture at Advancing Analytics:

“Regardless of your level... everyone's encouraged to speak up.”

You Don't Have to Know Everything to Start

Perhaps that's why Aoife’s advice to someone considering data today isn't simply to learn as many technologies as possible.

Yes, she talks about Python, SQL and Databricks. But the capability she describes as “priceless” is critical thinking. As AI increasingly helps people produce technical outputs, she believes the important human skill is being able to judge whether that output is actually correct, whether it addresses the problem you're trying to solve, and whether you understand the underlying business or technology problem well enough to make that judgement in the first place.

Communication matters just as much. Being able to take something deeply technical and explain it simply to somebody who isn't technical isn't an add-on to expertise in Aoife’s view. It is evidence that you genuinely understand what you're talking about. And perhaps that's reassuring for someone standing on the outside of the industry looking in.

You don't need to arrive knowing everything to start your data career.

Aoife certainly didn't. She arrived through astrophysics, discovered Python, experimented with data analysis, joined a graduate programme without knowing exactly where it would take her and landed in a profession she hadn't previously considered. She found something she loved, but it was the teams around her who helped her recognise just how far she could take it.

Making the Path More Visible for the Person Behind You

Stories like Aoife’s matter. Gender parity in data and AI can sound like a huge, abstract ambition, but careers are built at a much more human level: somebody being encouraged to try something at school, somebody discovering a career they didn't know existed, somebody seeing a woman ahead of them and realising progression is possible, somebody checking that their voice is being heard.

Advancing Analytics are proud partners of Women in Data® and hope that by sharing personal stories such as Aoife’s will help pave a route for somebody considering their career options behind them because “seeing that it's possible and being told you can do it” is where a career begins.

simon_willison:baaf713b11e3.title: Locating the source of a mysterious beep with Claude
simon_willison:baaf713b11e3.excerpt:
Our house has a box room, full of boxes that we still haven't unpacked from our last move. A couple of weeks ago something in that room started intermittently beeping. The beeps were far enough apart that standing in the room and trying to determine the source of the noise was frustrating, and I really didn't want to dig through every one of those boxes. So I had Claude Code build Beep Locator, a software system for triangulating the source of a mysterious beep using multiple devices scattered around the room.

Here's what Beep Locator looks like after it has been running for a while:

You run Python web server to show the primary UI, and then use the QR code or URL to connect as many devices as you can spare to act as listeners - I was using two iPads, a phone, a MacBook Pro and a Surface Ultra.

The devices then play noises to each other to help estimate their locations. This didn't work particularly well, so I added a "Rough mode" where you can drag their icons around in the space to provide rough locations which are then adjusted based on those sounds.

Once that's set up, the devices all listen for the beep!

I added a clapping mode too so I could test it by clapping my hands in different locations around the room - displayed as diamonds on the map. This helped me gain confidence that it was capable of locating a sound.

Beeps show up on the map as an X, plus a line in the "Sounds located" log. You can replay these sounds (from each device in turn) to confirm they are the mysterious beep you are looking for, then click "This is the mystery beep" to mark them as such.

Once you've confirmed the mysterious beep frequency the system will listen out for it, measure the interval between beeps, and use the triangulated locations to lock down the most likely location on the map.

The system worked as intended. It gave me the position of the beep to within about 40cm, then I dug through that specific pile of boxes and found an ancient carbon monoxide detector that desperately wanted its batteries replaced.

How it works

When I started working through this problem with Claude it quickly dug up BeepBeep: A High-Accuracy Acoustic-Based System for Ranging and Localization Using COTS Devices, a 2007 paper by Chunyi Peng, Guobin Shen, Yongguang Zhang, Yanlin Li, and Kun Tan. Here's that paper's abstract:

We present the design, implementation, and evaluation of BeepBeep, a high-accuracy acoustic-based ranging system. It operates in a spontaneous, ad-hoc, and device-to-device context without leveraging any pre-planned infrastructure. It is a pure software-based solution and uses only the most basic set of commodity hardware – a speaker, a microphone, and some form of device-to-device communication – so that it is readily applicable to many low-cost sensor platforms and to most commercial-off-the-shelf mobile devices like cell phones and PDAs. It achieves high accuracy through a combination of three techniques: two-way sensing, self-recording, and sample counting.

That sounded exactly like what we needed to build!

Beep Locator runs a Python web application server that does most of the work. The listening devices then connect to that server via WebSockets and present a UI which requests browser microphone access. The listeners mainly work by recording a 60 second buffer of recent audio. They also run a simple beep detection algorithm (see detector.js), which uses Fast Fourier Transform and a high-pass filter to identify potential beeps. It sends these events to the main server.

When a beep is reported, the server has a device play a short chirp (the device with the lowest round-trip time to the server), then asks every listener upload a clip from about 0.6s before the beep to 0.8s after that chirp. This chirp allows the clips to be aligned with each other, a crucial step in locating the beep.

How I built it

I started this project using Claude Code Cloud via my iPhone, with Opus 5.5 running in Extra thinking effort mode. Here's that shared starter session, which began with this prompt against a newly created empty GitHub repository:

Write out a problem.md file describing the problem we want to solve

There is a device beeping in a room and I cannot find it

I want to set up several devices - laptops, phones, iPads - around the room all listening at the same time and have them help triangulate where the beep comes from

There needs to be a Python web app which coordinates it all - one device shows a web page for the app, other devices join a URL which turns them into listeners - all via browser WebAudio and WebSockets back to the Python server app

Ideally I wouldn't need to manually input the relative locations of the devices - it would be amazing if they could play sounds to each other in order to locate each other in 2D space - is that even possible though?

That got me this problem.md file. As part of writing that up Claude found and read the BeepBeep paper, which is described in that file.

The research looked good, so I told it:

Ok try and build it, add a mechanism so you can send new code to the listeners which they will then run automatically - that way I can set everything up in the room and then leave you alone to continue hacking and experiment while I do something else

That got me to this point - most of the system was built, but nothing had actually tried running it yet.

I cloned the new repository to my laptop and fired up Claude Code... and then Fable 5.2 was released, and this project seemed like an excellent opportunity to put that through its paces.

I had Claude Code on my laptop start the server running, then made sure it could both see what was happening and make live changes to the software as it ran.

This was already baked into the software: Opus 5.5 had built an installModule() method on the listeners that could be triggered over the WebSocket connection, meaning the admin server could execute arbitrary new code on any of its clients.

On some devices, web pages that listen on the microphone request user permission any time the page reloads. The hot-swap module mechanism meant that we could deploy new code without having to manually interact with each of the listening devices in turn.

From that point on my involvement was mainly to sit by the laptop chatting with Fable 5.2 about what was going on, and occasionally requesting new features. Here are some of the feature prompts I ran:

I think we need to make it so I can drag things around on the map in “rough mode”, where my job is just to put them roughly where they are, then switch out of rough mode and it attempts to get them accurate

This gave me the ability to drag listeners around the map.

what’s a good way for me to test this I wonder? Can we have it listen for claps, then I could clap and it could identify the location of the clap? [...]

Claps should use a different symbol on the map than beeps

That added the thing where any time I clapped it would show on the map as a different symbol from the beeps.

each symbol on the map should include a HH:MM:SS timestamp

That made it easier to spot which symbol likely reflected which real-world sound.

The log should show beeps and claps with their timestamps AND have a little play button which, when clicked, replays the recorded noise from each of the listeners in sequence (with clear text on screen showing which listener recorded which snippet) while temporarily turning off microphone recording while that replay plays

Now I could replay sounds, making it much easier to identify which recorded clip was the mysterious beep I was looking for.

There should be a button next to a recording for “This is the mystery beep” - then I can hit replay to see and then confirm it was the mystery beep if that’s the one I am looking for

Then the system can categorize noises in the future to see if they are likely that same mysterious beep and use that information to build a more accurate idea of where it is

At this point I was getting close - I had a solid idea of where the beep was coming from, but wouldn't it be neat if I could reposition the listeners around that point to get an even finer location?

I want a feature for this, I don’t want to have to restart each listening device etc, I want to be able to click a “Reposition the devices” button which lets me switch into repositioning, then I click “Repositioned” and it puts me into Rough mode and asks me to roughly locate them, then I do that and click, then it starts up again. The previous session can be read-only viewed through the app.

And since I had one spare device, I then said:

add a feature where the map includes a spot that is a suggestion for a location that it would be useful to add a listener at - based on data collected so far

Giving Claude Code ears

I think the most interesting part of this project is that I demonstrated it's possible to give Claude Code ears.

Claude doesn't have native audio input (yet), but it can run JavaScript and Python code that can analyze audio captured by a microphone.

I told it to run a web server with WebSocket connections to multiple listening devices, then had it both run a WebAudio microphone on those devices and hook them up so they could be sent fresh JavaScript code to execute via that WebSocket.

Then I could pretty much leave Claude alone, hacking away at the problem, querying the audio logs, and reconfiguring its ears to help it solve the problem.

I'm reminded of a similar hack I heard about at GitHub Universe a few weeks ago, where Martin Woodward told me he had been debugging the GitHub Universe Badge computers by plugging them into a computer via USB-C and then pointing a webcam at their screen, so his coding agent could tell if updates were working correctly or not.

Figuring out ways to let coding agents perceive the world around them is a whole lot of fun.

simon_willison:6ee1dee33e4b.title: Hide your slop PR descriptions behind <details><summary>
simon_willison:6ee1dee33e4b.excerpt:
Most of the changes I make to my projects these days come in the form of PRs opened for me by Claude Code or Codex. The PR is my unit of work - I use them to bundle commits together, iterating on them until a feature is complete, document decisions and then merge the finished result. Today's coding agents are great at writing PR descriptions.

They're too good at describing the work

The problem is that they are too good. An agent-written PR description is accurate and comprehensive. It describes the problem, the detailed solution, and the steps taken to verify it. That's a lot of information to absorb.

It's not necessarily slop, but it reads like slop!

It's very easy to spot an AI-written PR, and as with other forms of AI writing my instant reaction is best summarized as "I'm not reading all of that". It doesn't matter how accurate or useful the information is, I'm instantly put off by the thought that it will take me longer to read than it took the driving author to write... even when that driving author is me!

I want human editorial judgement. I want someone to have thought just long enough about the PR to give me a human-approved introduction that helps me understand, at a high level, what the PR is for and whether it deserves more of my attention.

I think I've found a low-effort way to do this that feels right.

Hide most of it in a details/summary

The HTML <details><summary> elements render as a collapsed heading (the summary) that can be expanded to view the larger piece of text. The code looks like this:

<details>
  <summary>Claude Opus 5.5</summary>
  <h2>The hook</h2>
  Plugins implement <code>register_agent_reference_types(datasette)</code>...
</details>

When rendered, it looks like this:

Crucially, <details><summary> is supported in GitHub Markdown. You can drop those tags directly into an issue comment or PR description and GitHub will hide the details and display just the summary plus an expansion arrow.

I've started using this for my AI-generated pull requests.

The opening paragraph of my PRs will be carefully selected to act as a high-level explanation of what's going on - the shortest text a human can read that will help get them up to speed.

I'll sometimes throw in a screenshot as well, since images are often the best way to quickly illustrate a new feature.

The full agent-written essay then follows in a <details><summary>. I use the model name and often the effort level as that summary, to make it abundantly clear what is going on - "Claude Opus 5.5 Medium" for example.

My PRs don't feel nearly as sloppy now! The information is all still there, but a reader can glance at it and get the top, human-curated information without their eyes glazing over at multiple paragraphs of agent-written details.

I don't always write the introduction myself - sometimes the agent has given me what I need already, hidden away in the avalanche of other text. My promise to the reader is that the short opener will represent my human judgement as to what is definitely worth their time.

Here are some recent examples where I've used this pattern, including the opener I used:

  • datasette PR #3052: Redesign row page as a vertical list of fields - "The row page showed its single row as a one-row table. For wide tables, like a 46-column GitHub repos table, that scrolled far off to the right and left most of the page blank." (then a screenshot)
  • datasette PR #3043: Pagination bar showing which rows are on the current page - "Table pages that span more than one page now make it obvious where you are, and offer navigation at the top of the page as well as the bottom." (plus screenshot)
  • datasette PR #3042: Load edit-tools.js on demand via a small loader - "edit-tools.js (~220KB) was loaded on every table, row and database page, even for users who couldn't edit anything. Now only load it for users who can edit when they first interact with an edit feature (including mouse over an edit link)."
  • datasette-agent PR #51: register_agent_reference_types plugin hook - "Lets plugins add their own kinds of item to the # tagging in the chat composer using a new register_agent_reference_types(datasette) plugin hook." - pictured above.
  • llm PR #1838: Add llm openai endpoint add/list/remove/path commands - "Adds commands for managing the records in extra-openai-models.yaml, so OpenAI-compatible endpoints can be saved from the command line instead of by hand-editing YAML." - then copied --help output.

The mnemonic

I used to have trouble remembering the order of the tags - is it <details><summary> or <summary><details>?

Here are two tricks that helped me.

First, and most obviously, the <summary> is clearly the bit where you summarize the details. That's the tag for your line of text that can be clicked to expand - the <details> element must then wrap everything else.

An even better trick is to always refer to these two tags as "details-summary".

"details-summary" is two syllables followed by three syllables. That rolls off the tongue more smoothly than the three-two punch of "summary-details".

Say "details-summary" out loud just a few times and you'll never forget the order of the tags again.

(I still wish GitHub would add a button to their Markdown editor for this - partly to save me painstakingly typing it on my mobile keyboard, and partly to help spread the word to more GitHub users that this feature exists.)

dbt_core_releases:481b8274ffec.title: v2.0.0-dev.44-test-pypi
dbt_core_releases:481b8274ffec.excerpt:
2.0.0-dev.44

Released November 11, 2026

Features

  • [Lake Compute] Read AWS Databricks Unity Catalog tables using Databricks profile PAT/OAuth M2M credentials, declaration-aware validation, and dbt debug attach parity. Existing fs catalogs.yml entries continue to use type: unity. Existing local Unity attach options in config.lakecompute must move to config.duckdb; Lake Compute access is read-only and Unity model writes are unsupported.
  • [ClickHouse] Adds cluster support and distributed_table / distributed_incremental materializations. (#14580)
  • Accept Databricks use_materialization_v2 as a model config so a project or individual model can choose its materialization path
  • [ClickHouse] Adds support for grants and dbt clone (#14652, #14585)
  • [ClickHouse] Accept the ClickHouse table options on snapshots and tests, engine, order_by and disable_on_cluster on seeds, and settings on unit tests, in dbt_project.yml and node config.
  • [Lake Compute] Lake Compute models can now ref() Databricks table and incremental models stored as managed Delta, without setting catalog_name
  • Accept Databricks merge_actions_explicit config to supply the full WHEN … THEN block of a merge incremental model as raw SQL (#16835)

Fixes

  • Fixes array_construct bug for Databricks with new adapter-specific macro. (#15893)
  • Preserve BigQuery relation column types when rendering unit test fixtures. (#15961)
  • Support Iceberg snapshots by preserving table format metadata and Snowflake-compatible timestamp precision (#15776)
  • BigQuery: make the priority profile setting a schema enum instead of a string (#16021)
  • Honor Snowflake catalog-linked database identifier case sensitivity during static analysis. (#16389)
  • ClickHouse: list relations per schema so get_relation is served from the relation cache instead of one catalog query per relation (#16427)
  • BigQuery seeds now load correctly when dbt runs outside the project root by resolving data files from each seed's package root. (#16127)
  • Indexing a modules.re match object (m[1], m['name']) returns the group instead of an empty string, matching dbt-core (#16451)
  • run_results.json reports why a data test failed or warned ("Got 2 results, configured to fail if != 0") instead of just Error or Warn, matching dbt-core (#16408)
  • Databricks: avoid synchronous OPTIMIZE when only automatic liquid clustering is configured. (#16539)
  • Exclude connection-limit wait time from the execution time reported in run results (#15724)
  • Accept --resource-type all and --resource-type default on v2 commands (#16589)
  • Name unnamed Databricks primary and foreign keys deterministically so safer replace and incremental runs keep stable key names (#16603)
  • Lowercase Databricks catalog, schema, and table names in information_schema constraint and column mask lookups so mixed-case schemas find existing constraints (#16611)
  • Stop dropping and re-adding unchanged Databricks primary and foreign keys on incremental runs by comparing keys on name and columns (#16612)
  • Emit Databricks constraint ALTER statements in a stable sorted order on incremental runs, matching dbt-databricks (#16617)
  • Scope the Databricks foreign-key metadata lookup joins to the constraint's catalog and schema so a same-named constraint elsewhere in the catalog no longer makes incremental runs drop and re-add the foreign key (#16737)
  • dbt retry reports 'Nothing to do' and exits 0 when the previous run has no retryable nodes, matching dbt-core
  • Databricks snapshots now accept zorder and skip_optimize from every config source, including dbt_project.yml, so the post-snapshot OPTIMIZE honors them as in dbt-databricks (#16699)
  • Replace a Databricks Hive metastore table with a view without renaming the table, which fails for managed Delta tables on S3. (#16760)
  • [ClickHouse] persist_docs descriptions containing ';' reach the server intact: ClickHouse SQL is split by a ClickHouse-aware scanner ($tag$ heredocs, backslash escapes, comments) instead of the Databricks lexer (#14585)
  • [ClickHouse] Replacing a view falls back to drop + create on servers without atomic EXCHANGE support (filesystems without renameat2); existing dictionaries are typed as dictionary relations
  • dbt retry after a parse-time failure no longer retries nodes outside the original --select
  • Recognize Databricks type names such as string, int, tinyint and decimal(p,s) in the Column is_string, is_number, is_integer, is_float and is_numeric checks, and never widen Databricks string columns during snapshot column expansion (#16791)
  • Add support for Databricks GEOGRAPHY and GEOMETRY metadata (#14601)
  • Databricks views updated with view_update_via_alter now enforce model contracts and reject column masks and row filters on ALTER and no-op runs, and keep column comments after ALTER VIEW AS changes the query (#16882)
  • Add zone attribute to pytz timezone objects so modules.pytz.utc.zone and modules.pytz.timezone(...).zone return the timezone name (#16970)
  • Implement modules.pytz.all_timezones and modules.pytz.all_timezones_set (#16966)
  • Ensure column-level foreign_key constraints on versioned models create DAG dependencies (#17023)

Under the Hood

  • Add PyPI banner for dbt-oss mirroring the existing dbt-core banner, without the dbt-core namespace deprecation notice
  • Run Databricks seeds through a single materialization path regardless of use_materialization_v2, matching dbt-databricks. (#16523)
  • Drop the no-op create_indexes and adapter.commit() calls from the Databricks snapshot materialization, matching dbt-databricks. (#16532)

fabric_blog:9d75db3e383d.title: The next chapter for CI/CD in Fabric Warehouse (Preview)
fabric_blog:9d75db3e383d.excerpt:
Building and operating a data warehouse is increasingly a software engineering discipline. Teams want to develop warehouse changes in isolation, version them in Git, review them through pull requests, promote them safely across environments, and automate the entire process using their existing CI/CD systems.

Over the past several releases, we've been evolving CI/CD in Fabric Warehouse around that lifecycle:

  • DacFx established a common schema deployment foundation.
  • Pre, and post-deployment scripts expanded deployments beyond schema changes.
  • Warehouse Item Definition APIs opened the same lifecycle to automation.

Together, these investments are creating a more complete CI/CD lifecycle for Fabric Warehouse, from developing and versioning database changes to deploying and automating them across environments. Let’s take a closer look at how each capability moves that experience forward, what’s available today, and what we’re building next.

What we've delivered

Establishing a consistent deployment foundation with DacFx

The first challenge was making Warehouse deployments behave like database deployments, not artifact copies. A Warehouse contains state, data, dependencies, and relationships between database objects. Moving a change from development to production therefore requires understanding what changed and how those changes should be applied to the target database.

This is where DacFx became foundational to the experience. With Git Integration, it is represented as a SQL database project in source control. Developers can work using familiar Git practices such as branching, commits, and pull requests. When those changes are synchronized back to Fabric, DacFx understands the database model and determines the schema changes that need to be applied.

Figure: Git-based development workflow in Microsoft Fabric, enabling isolated feature development, collaboration through pull requests, and synchronization of Fabric items across feature and shared workspaces, with infrastructure managed as code.

We extended that same foundation to deployment pipelines. When a Warehouse moves between development, test and production environments, DacFx compares source and target states and generates the incremental deployment required to move the target to the desired state. 

Figure: End-to-end CI/CD workflow in Microsoft Fabric, combining Git-based feature development with deployment pipelines to promote Fabric items consistently across development, test, and production environments.

That established a consistent path: Develop → Version in Git → Review → Deploy → Validate → Promote.

Pre, and post-deployment scripts

A production deployment rarely consists of schema changes alone. Teams often need to prepare data before a deployment, seed or initialize data afterward, or execute SQL actions that need to happen at a specific point in the release. To support that workflow, we introduced pre, and post-deployment scripts.

A shared SQL query can be designated as a pre, or post-deployment script and becomes part of the SQL project. The designation travels with the Warehouse through Git, allowing those actions to be versioned and deployed together with the database definition. The resulting deployment lifecycle becomes pre-deployment actions → DacFx schema deployment → post-deployment actions

Figure: Pre, and post-deployment script configuration in Fabric Warehouse, enabling developers to define SQL scripts that execute automatically before and after schema deployment as part of the CI/CD lifecycle.

This moves more of the database release process into the CI/CD definition rather than leaving teams to coordinate separate manual steps. Learn more about pre and post-deployment scripts.

Warehouse Item Definition APIs

Git integration and deployment pipelines provide built-in Fabric experiences, but enterprise CI/CD also needs to work outside the Fabric portal. Customers have existing build systems, automation frameworks and release pipelines and need a programmatic way to manage Warehouse definitions.

Warehouse Item Definition APIs are the next part of that foundation. Warehouse definitions support SQL project and DACPAC formats, and Fabric APIs can be used to create a Warehouse from a definition, retrieve its current definition, or update it programmatically. Learn more about the Warehouse REST APIs. This means the same Warehouse definition that underpins Git integration can also participate in API-driven CI/CD workflows.

Bringing Familiar Warehouse Development Experiences to Client Tools

A complete CI/CD experience starts well before deployment. Developers need familiar tools to build, compare, validate, and manage database changes throughout the development lifecycle. Alongside our DacFx investments, we've strengthened Fabric Warehouse support across SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS) and Visual Studio Code, bringing familiar SQL development workflows closer to the Fabric web experience.

These investments include:

  • Database project support in SSMS: Develop and manage Warehouse schemas using SQL database projects and familiar database development workflows.
  • Schema Compare in VS Code: Compare database schemas, review differences, and generate the changes needed to synchronize environments.
  • Consistent database development: Use the same SQL project and DacFx foundation whether developing in the Fabric portal or client tools.
  • Pre, and post-deployment scripts: Maintain deployment scripts as part of the database project, enabling a consistent deployment experience across web-based and client-based development workflows.

The goal is simple: developers should be able to choose their preferred development environment without changing how their database projects are versioned, built, or deployed.

This brings together the flexibility of familiar SQL development tools with the integrated CI/CD experience in Fabric Warehouse.

What's next for CI/CD in Fabric Warehouse

Building on this foundation, we’re focusing on three investments:

  • Deployment configurations: Give developers control over how changes are applied. Cover data handling, object handling, and error handling. Apply different behaviors per environment, such as permissive in development and stricter in production.
  • Fabric CI/CD package (fabric-cicd) support for Warehouse: Simplify end-to-end automation. Deploy Warehouse definitions from source control alongside other Fabric items. Integrate with systems like Azure DevOps and GitHub Actions.
  • CI/CD for SQL analytics endpoint: Extend Git integration and deployment pipelines using the same SQL project and DacFx foundation. Lay the groundwork for coordinated deployments across dependent Fabric items in medallion and data mesh architectures.

The goal: Move from CI/CD for individual items to a consistent, predictable, automated lifecycle for interconnected Fabric analytics solutions.

Get started with CI/CD in Fabric Warehouse

  • Connect your Warehouse to Git: Set up Git integration to version your Warehouse as a SQL database project and develop changes in isolation.
  • Promote changes across environments: Use deployment pipelines to move Warehouse changes from development to test and production.
  • Automate data actions around your releases: Configure pre and post-deployment scripts so data preparation and seeding travel with your database definition.
  • Integrate with your existing CI/CD systems: Use the Warehouse REST APIs to create, retrieve, and update Warehouse definitions programmatically.

Try these capabilities today and share your feedback in Fabric Ideas | Microsoft Fabric Community. Your input directly shapes what we build next for CI/CD in Fabric Warehouse.

fabric_blog:9faf7642734c.title: Use OneLake as native storage for Azure Databricks (Preview)
fabric_blog:9faf7642734c.excerpt:
Organizations increasingly use Microsoft Fabric and Azure Databricks together so teams can choose the tools that best fit their data engineering, analytics, and AI workloads while working from a common data foundation.

OneLake external-location support for Azure Databricks Unity Catalog is now generally available in Microsoft Fabric, with OneLake Security enabled by default for Azure Databricks Storage items. On the Azure Databricks side, the feature is in preview.

With this integration, supported Unity Catalog-managed data can be stored directly in OneLake. To understand the setup and supported scenarios, Connect Azure Databricks to a OneLake external location.

Why this matters

Data teams often need Azure Databricks and Microsoft Fabric in the same architecture. Without a shared storage approach, organizations may create copies of the same data for different platforms, introduce pipelines whose primary purpose is synchronization, and manage access independently across multiple storage locations.

Using OneLake as managed storage for supported Unity Catalog objects gives organizations a common physical data foundation while preserving flexibility in the services used above it. Azure Databricks continues to provide compute and Unity Catalog management, while OneLake provides the storage destination and Fabric-side data-access controls.

What's new in this release

This release builds on the Beta announcement, which introduced OneLake external-location support for Unity Catalog.

OneLake Security is now enabled by default for Azure Databricks Storage items, so no user gets access when the item is created. Fabric workspace roles, including Admin, Member, and Contributor, cannot grant access to the data stored in Azure Databricks Storage item and managed through Unity Catalog. Only the Azure Databricks identity can read and write to Azure Databricks Storage items.

The updated security experience helps platform teams move from testing connectivity to planning controlled adoption. 

One shared data foundation, with flexibility above it

Use OneLake as the storage foundation

Azure Databricks workloads can create supported Unity Catalog-managed data directly in OneLake. A Unity Catalog external location points to an Azure Databricks Storage item in OneLake, and a catalog or schema can use that external location as managed storage.

Continue using Unity Catalog-managed objects

Teams can continue using Azure Databricks and Unity Catalog to create and manage supported managed tables, volumes, views, materialized views, and streaming tables. The objects remain managed through the Azure Databricks experience while their underlying supported data is stored in OneLake.

Keep platform responsibilities clear

Azure Databricks remains the environment for Databricks compute and Unity Catalog management. Microsoft Fabric provides the capacity-backed workspace and Azure Databricks Storage item, while OneLake provides the physical storage foundation.

How it works

  1. Provision storage in Microsoft Fabric: Create a capacity-backed Fabric workspace and an Azure Databricks Storage item. The storage item provides the OneLake location used by the integration.
  2. Configure the Azure Databricks identity: Use the managed identity of an Access Connector for Azure Databricks, or a service principal. Assign it the Viewer role on the Fabric workspace, then add it as the only member of a ReadWrite OneLake security role on the Azure Databricks Storage item.
  3. Create the Unity Catalog connection: In Azure Databricks, create a storage credential for the approved identity, and then create a OneLake external location that points to the Azure Databricks Storage item.
  4. Create Unity Catalog objects: Configure a catalog or schema to use the OneLake external location as managed storage. Data written by supported Azure Databricks workloads is then stored directly in OneLake.

Security 

OneLake security is enabled by default for the Azure Databricks storage item, so no user gets access when the item is created. Fabric workspace roles (Administrator, Member, Contributor, and Viewer) cannot grant access to the data in Azure Databricks storage item. To keep your data secure and under Unity Catalog governance:

  • Add only the Azure Databricks access connector's managed identity to the OneLake security role.
  • Do not add any other users, groups or service principals.
  • Fabric users should read data through mirrored items, not through the storage directly.

Only the Azure Databricks identity should access the storage item: Unity Catalog is the single place 
where you grant, review, and revoke access to the data.

How to read the data in Fabric 

Fabric users read the data through a mirrored Azure Databricks catalog item, not through the Azure 
Databricks Storage item. The mirrored catalog item shows the Unity Catalog catalogs, schemas, and 
tables you select in a Fabric workspace, without copying the data. Analysts and engineers can query it 
through the SQL analytics endpoint, notebooks, and Power BI reports.

You can create the mirrored catalog item from either platform: 

  • From Azure Databricks, with Publish to Fabric: Run it on the catalog you want to share, and it 
    creates the mirrored catalog item in the Fabric workspace you choose. This route suits data 
    engineers who already work in Azure Databricks. 
  • From Microsoft Fabric, as a new Mirrored Azure Databricks catalog item: Connect to your 
    Azure Databricks workspace, then choose the catalog, schemas, or tables to include. This route 
    suits Fabric administrators and analysts who manage the workspace.

Fabric readers use the mirrored catalog item. Never add them to the storage item's OneLake security 
role, which is reserved for the Azure Databricks identity.

Get started

Ready to use OneLake as managed storage for Azure Databricks Unity Catalog objects?

Start with the Connect Azure Databricks to a OneLake external location tutorial and plan your deployment.

azure_databricks_release_notes:d833d3fc8.excerpt:
In an upcoming release, Python Lakeflow pipelines will support partial schema inference in Beta. You will be able to use the override_schema argument of table, materialized_view, or create_streaming_table to declare only the columns whose type, constraint, or comment you want to control. azure_databricks_release_notes:672b8cfe5.excerpt:
You can now use the AI Functions Asynchronous API to run ai_parse_document, ai_extract, or ai_classify asynchronously on up to 50,000 requests from a JSONL file in a Unity Catalog volume. The batch writes one result for each request to a file in a volume. Workspace admins can turn on the AI Functions Asynchronous API preview from the Previews page. This feature is in Beta.

See the Asynchronous API reference. For examples, see document parsing, information extraction, and classification.

dbt_core_releases:3e4b9a281671.title: dbt v1.12.7
dbt_core_releases:3e4b9a281671.excerpt:
dbt-core 1.12.7 - November 12, 2026

Features

  • Extend RunResult with the state_decision_id attribute (#0)

Fixes

  • Fall back to per-source freshness checks when batch metadata freshness computation fails, instead of skipping every selected source now that skip_nodes_if_on_run_start_fails defaults to True (#15634)
  • Scope relation-cache population in compile/show/docs generate to the selected nodes' schemas so --cache-selected-only is honored (previously only run respected the flag) (#12944)
  • Fix statically_parse_unrendered_config stringifying list/dict config values, which caused false positives in state:modified comparisons across different dbt versions. (#16133)
  • Reword the snapshot timestamp data type mismatch warning to identify hard-delete timestamps as the affected columns and to recommend overriding the snapshot_get_time macro, instead of incorrectly suggesting a change to the snapshot's updated_at config (#fs-14450)
  • Recognize Databricks Python model config keys (access_control_list, notebook_access_control_list) in jsonschema validation so they no longer raise spurious CustomKeyInConfigDeprecation warnings (dbt-databricks#1661) (#N/A)
  • Add the builtin_macros_prefer_overrides behavior flag (default false). When enabled and the macro search package is itself internal (e.g. dbt or dbt_postgres, as for builtin macros run via adapter.execute_macro), the adapter override is preferred over the base dbt implementation and a root-project macro always wins. It is off by default because a root-project macro that shares a builtin's name can otherwise hijack calls made inside dbt's own macros. (#16540)
  • Accept the dbt v2-only info_schema, check-paths and checks keys in dbt_project.yml, ignoring them with a note that they are specific to the dbt v2 engine (#16640)
  • Ignore manifest nodes with resource types dbt-core doesn't support, such as dbt v2 checks, when loading a manifest for --state and --defer (#16849)
  • Supply credentials for dbt deps git packages through a git credential helper instead of embedding them in the clone URL, so clones of redirecting repositories keep working with libcurl 7.81.0-1ubuntu1.30 and later (#16861)
  • Recognize Databricks use_materialization_v2 config in JSON schema validation (#16879)
  • Fix dbt deps failing with "could not read Username" when installing a git package from a subdirectory with credentials in the URL, by supplying credentials to the checkout's git reset --hard as well (#16861)
  • Recognize supported dbt State configurations on snapshots and data tests during JSON schema validation (#N/A)

Dependencies

  • Bump dbt-core-experimental-parser lowerbound to 2.0.11 (#17117)

Contributors

  • @HannanNaeem (#fs-14450)
  • @aagarg (#16133)
  • @aahel (#16640, #16849)
  • @ash2shukla (#16861, #16861)

  • @dataders (#12944, #N/A)
  • @izeigerman (#0)

  • @piotrbator2 (#16540)
  • @sd-db (#N/A)

claude_code_releases:1e1f91e95e92.title: v2.1.323
claude_code_releases:1e1f91e95e92.excerpt:
What's changed

  • Added Code Mode, an experimental opt-in in which Claude writes JavaScript to call its tools; see https://code.claude.com/docs/en/code-mode to turn it on, or to turn it off for an organization
  • Added engines["claude-code"] to plugin.json: plugins outside their stated Claude Code version range are not installed, updated or loaded, and install and update pick the newest version that fits
  • Added type checking of a plugin's TypeScript hooks module to claude plugin validate; each finding is a warning, and --strict fails on it
  • Added to claude plugin validate the $ nouns a mod's engine.create hook adds, withholds or replaces
  • Added support for CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_MODE_MODEL in managed settings for Claude Desktop sessions on third-party providers (takes effect once Claude Desktop includes this version)
  • Added an options menu (stop, switch to usage credits, upgrade) when a model needs usage credits that are turned off or used up
  • Added a progress heartbeat every 30 seconds while hooks run long in claude -p and SDK sessions, so a host such as Claude Desktop won't end the turn as hung (once it includes this version)
  • Added .docx support to Artifact tool asset uploads
  • Added a /diff to close hint to the diff panel, and the keys that focus and close a panel to the ? shortcut guide
  • Added a start-up warning for Bash allow rules with a * in a variable's value, such as Bash(PORT=* npm run dev)
  • Added a warning when a plugin's language server can't start, naming the server and what to check
  • Added a one-time startup notice naming CLAUDE_CODE_PERFORCE_MODE when Perforce settings are found and the mode is off
  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AGENT_PROGRESS_SUMMARIES (available since 2.1.318): set it to 1 to turn off subagent progress summaries and the requests that write them (#86879)
  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_RESUME_HINT_COMMAND, which a program that starts Claude Code can set to have the exit hint name its own resume command
  • Added unsetOptionCount to the claude plugin install --json result: how many userConfig options are not yet set
  • Added isPromptCovered to the props a mod's pane is drawn with, telling it when a dialog or a field above the prompt covers the prompt
  • Fixed running /compact again, or after a command such as /context, summarizing away a message that Claude had not answered yet
  • Fixed a resumed session joining your next message to an old interrupted message that was not resumed
  • Fixed a memory spike at the next prompt after Claude changed a very large file
  • Fixed a setting saved in a running session undoing a hand edit made to settings.json moments earlier; a settings file you delete during a session now stays deleted
  • Fixed claude plugin commands and claude mcp list signing you out of a Console profile when they ended while the token was being renewed
  • Fixed Edit and Bash running out of memory on certain /proc files, and Edit hanging or running out of memory on devices and named pipes
  • Fixed Claude Code failing to start, or to clear stored credentials at sign-out, when saving its configuration file failed with "Out of memory"
  • Fixed requests sent without streaming failing on errors that streamed requests recover from, such as a rejected image, thinking block or beta header
  • Fixed ExitWorktree, the worktree exit dialog and /resume leaving the session in the wrong folder when the folder the shell was in before entering the worktree had been deleted
  • Fixed accents and other combining marks sometimes landing left of the text, leaving stale copies on screen, or silently disappearing when text wraps
  • Fixed the last key of a key chord, such as Enter in ctrl+x enter, acting on a dialog's text field when the chord's own action isn't available there
  • Fixed ps processes piling up when the process listing Claude Code runs before stopping a command takes too long
  • Fixed subagent transcripts and large tool results being saved apart from the session's transcript after entering a worktree created by a WorktreeCreate hook or belonging to a nested repository
  • Fixed a session on a named Anthropic profile moving to another sign-in when /fork, the Left arrow or --bg continued it in the background; reopen any session that was open during the update
  • Fixed a background session sending a conversation under another sign-in when its named Anthropic profile is missing, changed or overridden; it now stops and says so
  • Fixed a session on an API key, auth token or workload identity from its shell (not a setup token) moving to another sign-in in the background; it now stops and says so
  • Fixed MCP tool calls ending in the sign-in server's error, such as TOKEN_EXPIRED, instead of asking you to sign in again
  • Fixed an expired claude.ai login showing "Credit balance too low" when a saved Console key or ant auth login profile without credit was used instead
  • Fixed a session on a named Anthropic profile being handed to an older background service that could not keep its sign-in; it now says to restart the service
  • Fixed a background session's sign-in leaving the previous account's login or other credentials in place; it now clears them for every session on the computer, and a refused sign-in can leave no login
  • Fixed background sessions moving between a profile and the stored login when an update restarted them
  • Fixed sessions opened before a sign-in keeping signed-out feature flags after the sign-in
  • Fixed sessions that kept failing after a Claude apps gateway sign-in expired: once you sign in again with /login in another terminal, they carry on at the next message
  • Fixed the billing notice naming your ant auth login organization when a custom X-Api-Key header is set
  • macOS: Fixed "Not logged in · Please run /login" coming back right after a successful /login or a token refresh when the keychain was slow to answer
  • Fixed turns failing in Claude Desktop when an organization's gateway answers an expired token with 403: Claude Code now asks Desktop for a fresh token and retries
  • Fixed the error shown when Amazon Bedrock refuses your account a model: it no longer says to refresh your AWS credentials, it says to enable the model
  • Fixed the awsAuthRefresh or gcpAuthRefresh command sometimes running twice for one request when three or more sessions needed a fresh sign-in at once
  • Fixed the claude -p warning about an ended claude.ai login to say that claude auth logout also removes saved MCP server logins and plugin secrets
  • Fixed Bash permission prompts offering "don't ask again" for commands that write to sensitive paths such as .git or .claude, where the saved rule did not stop the next prompt
  • Fixed a case where some lsof commands ran without a permission prompt
  • Fixed Bash commands that write a file with cat > file <<EOF being shown as "Read 1 file"

  • Improved sign-in errors in /login and claude setup-token for a rejected, unreachable or timed-out request: they now say what happened and what to check
  • Improved Bash permission checks so the same command more reliably gets the same answer on a slow or busy machine
  • Improved Bash permission checks: some commands that could run differently from how they were checked now ask for permission
  • Improved /mcp to show how many of a server's tools were left out because the API would reject their input schema, and why
  • Improved the "Not now" choice when Claude Code asks to turn on the mods it writes in a session: it now says when they load
  • Improved the error for an MCP tool call whose connector ID is mistyped by a character or two: for a server that the host application registered, it now names the tool to call
  • Improved Claude Desktop and cloud sessions for claude.ai accounts with more than 2,000 plugins turned on: a shorter wait at startup, and Claude can now say why plugins are missing
  • Improved memory use with many subagents: a finished subagent's transcript is freed sooner instead of staying in memory while later subagents run
  • Improved installing with the install script: the latest version is no longer downloaded twice
  • Improved WebFetch speed and memory use on deeply nested pages
  • Improved the cleanupPeriodDays cleanup to count folders it can't read as errors
  • Improved the Claude apps gateway's /v1/models to state max_input_tokens for models whose context window is certain on every upstream
  • Improved ToolSearch to say when a tool Claude searched for by its short name is already available, instead of only reporting no match
  • Improved start-up on Linux when /home is an autofs map: Claude Code no longer looks up files in /home itself. Set CLAUDE_CODE_AUTOMOUNT_ROOTS for a map root deeper than one folder below /
  • Improved the Fable limit message in -p, SDK, IDE and cloud sessions: it now says when the limit resets, along with how to continue
  • Changed /security-review to ask before Claude runs it, and skills' inline git commands to stop in bare-repository worktrees and similar folders until you allow them, outside auto mode and bypass
  • Changed how many messages each of your sessions on the same machine can send the others without a prompt from you, from about 20 to 100,000
  • Changed the number of messages a Claude Desktop Code tab session can send to your other sessions before it waits for you to type again from 20 to 100,000
  • Changed organization settings and policy requests to no longer use a proxy set only by ALL_PROXY; set HTTPS_PROXY if your network needs a proxy for them
  • Changed the context window assumed for a model ID that Claude Code doesn't recognize from 200K to 1M; use /autocompact to compact earlier, or CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_1M_CONTEXT=1 to keep 200K
  • Changed sessions on other vendors' models with a smaller window: once full, they can fail every turn until /clear, so set CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_1M_CONTEXT=1 before they fill
  • Changed Claude Code's own ripgrep and most internal git commands to run without most of its sign-in tokens and API keys, so a credential helper or hook under such a git command no longer finds them
  • Changed MCP_SDK_GENERATION=v1 to run the v2 MCP client in a compatibility mode (earlier handshake, relaxed OAuth sign-in checks), because the v1 MCP client is removed
  • Changed the tool Claude uses to finish an MCP server sign-in so that it asks you to confirm, even in bypass and auto modes; where nobody can be asked, such as in dontAsk mode, use /mcp
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed a session at a connector's approval prompt or sign-in inside a running tool to be released as paused at the idle or lifetime limit; a late answer resumes from a fresh clone
  • Changed artifact updates to ask first, even under an allow rule, when people outside your organization can see the artifact or Claude can't check who can
  • Changed glab config set without --global or --host, and glab config edit --local, to fail read-only inside the Bash sandbox; run them outside it
  • Changed the Bash sandbox on macOS, Linux and WSL to ignore write access granted through a symlink in a writable folder that leads elsewhere or to a missing path; grant the real path instead
  • Changed "don't ask again" so an allow rule that looks like it holds a secret, or would be saved to a settings.local.json that git tracks, lasts for the session only and isn't saved
  • Changed the sandbox on macOS and Linux: git worktree add, move and remove now fail read-only, as do commits in a worktree the session wasn't started in or given, even one inside the project
  • Changed start-up to stop when a --settings file isn't valid JSON and has a sandbox key, even one that turns the sandbox off
  • Changed what happens when a tool's permission check fails with an error after a PreToolUse hook returned "allow": Claude Code now decides the call as if no hook had answered
  • Changed what happens when a tool's permission check fails on input that a PermissionRequest hook rewrote: Claude Code now asks again, or refuses the call where nobody can answer
  • Changed the GitLab merge request badge to show only for the repository a sandboxed session opened in
  • Changed the claude mcp add --help example to a local command
  • Changed mods: a *, namespace or negated hook on engine.create now only observes. To add or withhold a $ noun, hook engine.create by name
  • Changed claude plugin validate to fail a mod whose engine.create hook isn't written in the one accepted form; installed mods keep loading
  • Changed marketplace and plugin installs to fail when a git submodule isn't on the commit its repository records
  • Changed project (.mcp.json) MCP server approvals to match the server's exact name; an approval entry written in another spelling now asks again
  • Changed self-hosted runners under --trust-workspace false and VS Code sessions in an untrusted folder: the repository's settings can no longer disable your hooks or turn plugins on or off
  • Changed tool.list plugin hooks so the tools they add or remove apply to the model and every agent
  • Changed claude plugin install and /plugin to show a warning instead of success when a plugin's install command writes to stderr
  • Changed claude.ai chats and Cowork tasks to check a plugin file for secret keys before sending it, and to ask first if it may hold one
  • Changed claude rm and the agents view to say a session is removed from the list, not deleted; claude rm help says the conversation is kept and claude --resume lists it
  • Changed /stickers to say that the sticker pack is all claimed for now, instead of opening a page in the browser
  • Changed a managed settings policyHelper to no longer take environment variables from user or --settings files; set what it needs in managed env or the launching shell
  • Changed a /skill or @file typed between two files picked in claude.ai or the desktop app, or after a picked file and a link, to no longer take effect
  • Changed split-pane agent teammates to check that requests come from their team lead: one that outlives its lead has its asks refused, and plan approvals must be re-sent after /clear or /resume
  • Changed worktree creation to refuse checkouts whose .git folders are links or hold hard links, such as git-new-workdir layouts and cp -al copies; use a plain clone
  • Changed what Claude is told after safeguards stop a forked skill or a workflow agent: retry with a narrower prompt or tell you, instead of doing the work itself
  • Changed browser tool calls (Claude in Chrome, the desktop browser pane) to refuse some escaped or JSON-text inputs and tell Claude how to respell them
  • Changed workflows so that a prompt an app marks as not typed no longer reaches their agents as your request
  • Changed computer use on macOS to refuse key chords that hold Space with Control or Option, and more system shortcuts that need your grant
  • Changed first-run setup in Terminal.app to name the "Use Option as Meta key" setting, what Option stops typing, and how to undo it before you agree
  • Changed the maximum of CLAUDE_CODE_OVERLOADED_RETRY_MAX_DELAY_MS from 64000 to 300000
  • Changed workflows in the desktop app's Code tab to pause at a usage limit and continue after it resets
  • Changed the spend limit and 1M context errors, and /usage-credits, in cloud sessions and under Remote Control: they no longer give a web address
  • Changed which MCP servers are reported by name in OpenTelemetry exports to follow the current connector directory
  • Changed /logout in a background session, which had no effect: it now signs out every session on the computer, deletes stored MCP logins and plugin secrets, and ends the session, as in a terminal
  • macOS: Changed the Bash sandbox so lsof and similar tools may show less about processes a command did not start
  • Changed cloud scheduled tasks: a PostToolUse hook from your own settings can no longer replace the plan in ExitPlanMode's result
  • Changed CLAUDE_AUTOCOMPACT_PCT_OVERRIDE in Anthropic-hosted cloud sessions to stop applying to auto-memory extraction and, in some sessions, to /btw; the main conversation still follows it
  • Removed the subagentStatusLine setting: subagent rows always use the default look, and settings files that still hold the key load as before
  • Deprecated a plugin's agent setting: it still applies, and now warns at startup, in claude plugin list and in claude plugin validate

fabric_blog:7a5707196999.title: Use OneLake as native storage for Azure Databricks
fabric_blog:7a5707196999.excerpt:
Organizations increasingly use Microsoft Fabric and Azure Databricks together so teams can choose the tools that best fit their data engineering, analytics, and AI workloads while working from a common data foundation.

OneLake external-location support for Azure Databricks Unity Catalog is now generally available in Microsoft Fabric, with OneLake Security enabled by default for Azure Databricks Storage items. On the Azure Databricks side, the feature is in preview.

With this integration, supported Unity Catalog-managed data can be stored directly in OneLake. To understand the setup and supported scenarios, Connect Azure Databricks to a OneLake external location.

Why this matters

Data teams often need Azure Databricks and Microsoft Fabric in the same architecture. Without a shared storage approach, organizations may create copies of the same data for different platforms, introduce pipelines whose primary purpose is synchronization, and manage access independently across multiple storage locations.

Using OneLake as managed storage for supported Unity Catalog objects gives organizations a common physical data foundation while preserving flexibility in the services used above it. Azure Databricks continues to provide compute and Unity Catalog management, while OneLake provides the storage destination.

What's new in this release

This release builds on the Beta announcement, which introduced OneLake external-location support for Unity Catalog.

OneLake Security is now enabled by default for Azure Databricks Storage items, so no user gets access when the item is created. Fabric workspace roles, including Admin, Member, and Contributor, cannot grant access to the data stored in Azure Databricks Storage item and managed through Unity Catalog. Only the Azure Databricks identity can read and write to Azure Databricks Storage items.

The updated security experience helps platform teams move from testing connectivity to planning controlled adoption. 

One shared data foundation, with flexibility above it

Use OneLake as the storage foundation

Azure Databricks workloads can create supported Unity Catalog-managed data directly in OneLake. A Unity Catalog external location points to an Azure Databricks Storage item in OneLake, and a catalog or schema can use that external location as managed storage.

Continue using Unity Catalog-managed objects

Teams can continue using Azure Databricks and Unity Catalog to create and manage supported managed tables, volumes, views, materialized views, and streaming tables. The objects remain managed through the Azure Databricks experience while their underlying supported data is stored in OneLake.

Keep platform responsibilities clear

Azure Databricks remains the environment for Databricks compute and Unity Catalog management. Microsoft Fabric provides the capacity-backed workspace and Azure Databricks Storage item, while OneLake provides the physical storage foundation.

How it works

  1. Provision storage in Microsoft Fabric: Create a capacity-backed Fabric workspace and an Azure Databricks Storage item. The storage item provides the OneLake location used by the integration.
  2. Configure the Azure Databricks identity: Use the managed identity of an Access Connector for Azure Databricks, or a service principal. Assign it the Viewer role on the Fabric workspace, then add it as the only member of a ReadWrite OneLake security role on the Azure Databricks Storage item.
  3. Create the Unity Catalog connection: In Azure Databricks, create a storage credential for the approved identity, and then create a OneLake external location that points to the Azure Databricks Storage item.
  4. Create Unity Catalog objects: Configure a catalog or schema to use the OneLake external location as managed storage. Data written by supported Azure Databricks workloads is then stored directly in OneLake.

Security 

OneLake security is enabled by default for the Azure Databricks storage item, so no user gets access when the item is created. Fabric workspace roles (Administrator, Member, Contributor, and Viewer) cannot grant access to the data in Azure Databricks storage item. To keep your data secure and under Unity Catalog governance:

  • Add only the Azure Databricks access connector's managed identity to the OneLake security role.
  • Do not add any other users, groups or service principals.
  • Fabric users should read data through mirrored items, not through the storage directly.

Only the Azure Databricks identity should access the storage item: Unity Catalog is the single place 
where you grant, review, and revoke access to the data.

How to read the data in Fabric 

Fabric users read the data through a mirrored Azure Databricks catalog item, not through the Azure 
Databricks Storage item. The mirrored catalog item shows the Unity Catalog catalogs, schemas, and 
tables you select in a Fabric workspace, without copying the data. Analysts and engineers can query it 
through the SQL analytics endpoint, notebooks, and Power BI reports.

You can create the mirrored catalog item from either platform: 

  • From Azure Databricks, with Publish to Fabric: Run it on the catalog you want to share, and it 
    creates the mirrored catalog item in the Fabric workspace you choose. This route suits data 
    engineers who already work in Azure Databricks. 
  • From Microsoft Fabric, as a new Mirrored Azure Databricks catalog item: Connect to your 
    Azure Databricks workspace, then choose the catalog, schemas, or tables to include. This route 
    suits Fabric administrators and analysts who manage the workspace.

Fabric readers use the mirrored catalog item. Never add them to the storage item's OneLake security 
role, which is reserved for the Azure Databricks identity.

Get started

Ready to use OneLake as managed storage for Azure Databricks Unity Catalog objects?

Start with the Connect Azure Databricks to a OneLake external location tutorial and plan your deployment.

azure_databricks_release_notes:3926e1860.title: OneLake external locations support file events (Public Preview)
azure_databricks_release_notes:3926e1860.excerpt:
You can now enable file events on OneLake external locations through a Fabric eventstream. Azure Databricks can create the eventstream for you, or you can provide your own.

See Set up file events.

azure_databricks_release_notes:e1fe74e2c.title: Importing Power BI and Tableau files with Genie Code will soon be available by default for workspaces with the compliance security profile enabled
azure_databricks_release_notes:e1fe74e2c.excerpt:
You can use Genie Code to import Power BI and Tableau files as AI/BI dashboards and metric views. Starting on or after December 15, 2026, this will be available by default for workspaces with the compliance security profile enabled. Until then, a workspace admin can turn it on from Previews in the workspace settings.

Importing requires partner-powered AI features for the account and workspace.

See Import BI files using Genie Code.

azure_databricks_release_notes:d38e75a03.title: Artifacts and slides in Genie One (Beta)
azure_databricks_release_notes:d38e75a03.excerpt: Artifacts are slide decks and other custom visual pages that Genie One builds from your data and saves to your workspace. Ask Genie for an artifact in chat, edit it yourself or ask for changes, then present it and share it with others. Anyone who views an artifact can use Ask Genie to ask questions about the data behind a chart or number. An artifact stores a snapshot of its data, so anyone who can view it sees that data, even without access to the source tables. This feature is in Beta. A workspace admin turns on the Artifacts preview from the Previews page. See Artifacts in Genie One and Slides in Genie One.

azure_databricks_release_notes:b8aff8f35.title: Connectors section in Genie Agent settings (Beta)
azure_databricks_release_notes:b8aff8f35.excerpt: The Configure settings for a Genie Agent now have a dedicated section for adding connectors. This feature is in Beta. See Add connectors to a Genie Agent.

azure_databricks_release_notes:410ab7f92.title: Genie One desktop app is generally available on macOS
azure_databricks_release_notes:410ab7f92.excerpt: The Genie One desktop app is now generally available on macOS. The app opens Genie One in its own window, with the same capabilities as the web experience plus desktop conveniences like window navigation controls, automatic updates, and a dock badge for unread activity. The Windows app is in Beta. See Use Genie One on desktop.

azure_databricks_release_notes:29d0c7ba5.title: Scheduled tasks can email other users in Genie One
azure_databricks_release_notes:29d0c7ba5.excerpt: Scheduled tasks in Genie One can now send emails to other users in your organization, not just to you. See Scheduled tasks.

azure_databricks_release_notes:9b07e0e6a.title: Use Genie One as your Chrome new tab page (Beta)
azure_databricks_release_notes:9b07e0e6a.excerpt: The Genie One Chrome extension replaces the Chrome new tab page with Genie One from your Azure Databricks workspace. While the extension is turned on, new tabs open the Genie One home page, so you can ask a question, search across your connected tools, or open a dashboard without first going to your workspace. The extension uses your existing Azure Databricks sign-in and permissions, and it works with the one workspace you choose. This feature is in Beta. See Use Genie One as your Chrome new tab page.

azure_databricks_release_notes:5f42b2f64.title: Postgres 18.7, 17.12, and 16.16 now available
azure_databricks_release_notes:5f42b2f64.excerpt: Lakebase updated its supported Postgres versions to 18.7, 17.12, and 16.16, less than 30 minutes after the PostgreSQL community released them. These minor releases include the latest upstream Postgres bug fixes and security patches. Lakebase applies a new minor version the next time your compute restarts. See Recent minor version rollouts.

azure_databricks_release_notes:50f2a26f4.title: Flows are securable objects in Unity Catalog (Beta)
azure_databricks_release_notes:50f2a26f4.excerpt: Pipeline flows are now securable objects in Unity Catalog. You can grant READ FLOW, REFRESH FLOW, WRITE FLOW, APPLY TAG, and MANAGE on individual flows, and CREATE FLOW on schemas. To participate in the Beta, contact your Databricks account team. azure_databricks_release_notes:438c7d259.excerpt:
OAuth on-behalf-of (OBO) for service principals is now generally available and turned on by default. With OBO, you use the standard user-to-machine (U2M) OAuth flow to act as a service principal you manage, without creating an OAuth secret. claude_code_releases:3578b3def025.title: v2.1.325
claude_code_releases:3578b3def025.excerpt:
What's changed

  • Fixed a security issue in how zstd-compressed responses are decoded
  • Added a spinner tip in VS Code and similar integrated terminals about re-running a notebook cell, shown once Claude has read or edited a Jupyter notebook
  • Added a line under the error shown when your organization's policy blocks a request, saying how to continue: run /rewind and change the message, or run /clear
  • Added a note for Claude when a sandboxed git checkout, git stash or autostash pull cannot update protected files such as those in .claude
  • Fixed /security-review and skills' inline git commands stopping with an error in worktrees of bare repositories, --separate-git-dir checkouts and Android repo checkouts
  • Fixed subagents with their own model being moved to the plan-mode model when the model setting is opusplan or haiku
  • Fixed subagents on a different model sizing file reads and MCP results with the main session's model
  • Fixed sessions on many third-party gateways and Foundry stopping with a context length error on every turn instead of compacting
  • Fixed recent turns sometimes going missing from a resumed session after Claude Code stopped without a clean exit
  • Fixed shell commands running in the launch directory after the working directory was deleted; the command now fails with a message and can be re-issued
  • Fixed an approved plan edit being lost when the plansDirectory folder can't take it: the plan is now saved in the default plans folder, and a warning says where and why
  • Fixed a saved sonnet[1m] model setting being rewritten on a new install to a model id the API rejects
  • Fixed focus view hiding the reply to your prompt when a scheduled task replied after it
  • Fixed the prompt sometimes missing from a background subagent's view when fullscreen is off
  • Fixed long options in lists and permission prompts being partly overwritten when they wrap, and first-run screens losing lines on narrow terminals
  • Fixed startup warnings about permission rules and the "N MCP servers need authentication" notice being recorded as seen when they were scrolled out of view
  • Fixed the welcome header showing control characters or splitting across lines when an agent's name or the working folder contains them or a line break
  • Fixed the red error shown when Claude tries a command only you can run: a dim line now says it runs only when you type it at the prompt
  • Fixed /stats showing an Active days total that was one day too high
  • Fixed /insights saying a report was ready when no session qualified for analysis, and writing two values into its HTML report without escaping them
  • Fixed /voice saying voice mode changed when managed settings, --settings, or the project's .claude/settings.json or .claude/settings.local.json kept it as it was; it now says what holds it
  • Fixed the IDE welcome dialog showing Cmd+Esc for Quick Launch on Windows and Linux

  • Fixed leftover .oauth_refresh.lock.owner.tmp.* files piling up in the config directory
  • Fixed /fast saying "Fast mode has been disabled by your organization" under the keyless Console sign-in, where Claude Code had not asked the server
  • Fixed /model saying that your organization restricts a model when Claude Code could not check that, for example with no network
  • Fixed "Sign in with your Console account" in /login replacing your existing login when you pressed Esc right after the browser step
  • Fixed the browser showing the sign-in success page in some cases where sign-in failed or was canceled
  • Fixed claude auth status and other short commands leaving a lock behind on a Console profile, which made the next session hang for about a minute
  • Fixed background sessions started on your claude.ai login using (and billing) an API key or token from the shell that started the background service

  • Fixed a session sometimes going back to an earlier permission mode after a subagent's plan was approved
  • Fixed one invalid value in an Agent SDK applyFlagSettings() call silently discarding all settings from earlier calls; a call that would do this is now refused with an error
  • Fixed sessions showing as waiting for input when a finished pull request only needed your own review or merge

  • Fixed --worktree skipping a WorktreeCreate hook from a plugin in CLAUDE_CODE_PLUGIN_SEED_DIR on the first run in a new home directory
