  • Fixed Claude saying a working Atlassian, Asana or Sentry connector had failed in cloud sessions when a plugin listed it at a different URL
  • Fixed Claude Desktop and SDK sessions listing a folder's own MCP servers (.mcp.json, local) as host-added or not at all, and not connecting WebSocket ones, after a folder move or pre-warmed start
  • Fixed /mcp still listing a plugin's MCP server after a plugin reload removed it while it was connecting
  • Fixed an MCP server staying "needs authentication", and its mcp_tool hooks being skipped, after a token refresh that was refused only for a moment
  • Fixed MCP elicitation requests being cancelled without asking in headless mode after a server's connection was replaced during a tool call
  • Fixed MCP tool calls from an SDK host answering "Not connected" after a tool call had reconnected the MCP server
  • Fixed an MCP task getting stuck after its question was closed with Esc or asked again: the footer now says it needs your input, and Enter in /tasks shows the question again
  • Fixed background MCP tasks that stopped updating after another call to the same server lost the connection, when a later call reconnects
  • Fixed a background MCP task's question opening over a message you were still typing; it now waits until you send or clear the draft, and the spinner and turn timer keep running

  • Fixed self-hosted runner sessions with several repositories being unable to use a repository added mid-session
  • Fixed Claude asking for permission before reading your own artifact or its data
  • Fixed deny and ask permission rules and hooks for the Artifact tool not applying in some cloud sessions
  • Fixed Code Mode scripts ignoring a worktree entered with EnterWorktree, writing ~ paths into the project, and leaving /mcp showing an MCP server as connected after its sign-in expired

  • Fixed some deny and ask rules not applying to certain Bash commands

  • Fixed some artifact publishes skipping the confirmation for pages that people outside your organization can see when "don't ask again" had been chosen for Artifact
  • Fixed auto mode judging only the first change to an artifact that people outside your organization can see; its yes now covers that change alone
  • Fixed a managed strictPluginOnlyCustomization lock on agents and skills not taking effect in sessions that were already running
  • Fixed sandboxed commands being able to write to the native updater's download folder in some cases
  • Fixed a case where the Bash sandbox did not fully protect a worktree's settings and hooks
  • Fixed a case where the Bash sandbox did not fully protect a linked worktree's shared git folder
  • Fixed /teleport's stash choice in some unusual git states: it now stops and says what to do
  • Windows: Fixed a start-up stall that could last about a second when a PATH entry sits under a folder your account cannot open
  • Fixed /resume on Windows refusing or hiding sessions whose folder was recorded with a different drive-letter case or slashes
  • Fixed an in-session /resume on Windows dropping a project's saved trust when the session was recorded with a different drive-letter case
  • Linux: Fixed sandboxed Bash commands failing with bwrap: Can't create file when the working directory was below an allowRead folder inside a denyRead, such as under a symlinked home directory
  • Fixed Claude Desktop's third-party deployments staying on "Stopping" until a token renewal finished (once it includes this version)
  • Improved subagents cut off at the output token limit: they are now asked for the whole answer again, more briefly, instead of returning only its end
  • Improved startup with a keyless Console sign-in or other Anthropic profile login: a token that is still valid is read without waiting for the credentials lock
  • Improved the account email check: it now also refuses your email as a client's identity in scripts a command runs, file writes, web fetches and MCP calls
  • Improved the HTTPS authentication failed message for private plugin marketplaces: it now says git's terminal prompts and askpass programs are disabled, and it also appears with newer git versions
  • Improved the add-marketplace confirmations, plugin recommendation prompts and plugin install warning to say that plugins can run code on your computer, with access to your files and shell
  • Improved the claude --desktop sign-in error to name the API key, provider or setting that stops a Claude account sign-in from working
  • Improved the /voice "No audio detected" message on macOS and Windows: it now says where to pick your microphone
  • Improved MCP tasks: Claude is now told when a task is waiting for your answer, and can point you to /tasks
  • Improved claude remote-control: it now exits with status 4 when it stops by itself (single-session runs still exit 0) and 69 when it can't register, so a service manager can start it again
  • Improved the messages shown when a background session can't use its session's API key or token: they no longer suggest adding the key to settings
  • Improved the bundled dataviz skill's part-to-whole advice for static images and for parts with a natural order, such as age bands
  • Changed sandboxed Bash commands to follow the normal permission flow by default; set sandbox.autoAllowBashIfSandboxed: true to keep running them without prompts
  • Changed managed settings that turn the sandbox on: to keep commands running without prompts, set sandbox.autoAllowBashIfSandboxed: true in your highest-ranking managed source
  • Changed read-only git commands to ask first in a repository that isn't the project's or one you trusted; name it with --add-dir, not the additionalDirectories setting, to run them without prompts
  • Changed scheduled tasks and /loop to ask before running a skill that declares allowed-tools or hooks; add Skill(name) to permissions.allow to run it unattended
  • Changed "Always allow" in Desktop, IDE and SDK hosts: a rule alone is offered only when saving it would allow that command again, so a scheduled task that relied on one can now wait for you

  • Removed "ask your admin to raise it" from spend limit and shared budget errors in cloud sessions and under Remote Control

  • [VSCode] Fixed the effort selector offering levels above the effort cap set by your organization or the maxEffortLevel setting

  • [VSCode] Fixed the permission prompt for MCP tools not saying why Claude Code asks when a safety check raises the question

simon_whiteley:ea585dd9c0fa.title: System One: Jev, ai_decide or Decisions API?
simon_whiteley:ea585dd9c0fa.excerpt:
Every day brings another System One release: a new TypeSafe AI Jev, ai_decide, OpenAI's Decisions API, Kev or OpenJev, each with a leaderboard of scores. They all do the same job: instead of writing an answer, they pick one from options you define and tell you how sure they are. New to System One models? This video walks through the basics and how to get started with Jev.

This excercise started with a simple question someone asked me: when should we use Jev or Databricks' ai_decide? With OpenAI's new Decisions API, it becomes:

Which hosted decision API should we use?

The headline

On easy calls all three are level. On fine-grained tasks, Jev and OpenAI's Decisions API stay level with each other and well ahead of ai_decide. Add examples to the prompt and Jev pulls ahead on the hardest job.

  Triage: broad intent Triage: exact case Next action
Jev 0.87 0.79 0.56
Jev + examples 0.91 0.87 0.71
ai_decide 0.86 0.70 0.39
ai_decide + examples 0.91 0.73 0.43
OpenAI Decisions 0.88 0.79 0.57
OpenAI Decisions + examples 0.92 0.86 0.63

Data: accuracy on 300 unseen test chats (the setup)
Scale: always guessing the most common next action scores 0.21

The setup

The data. The Action-Based Conversations Dataset (ABCD; Chen et al., 2021): about 10,000 role-played customer-support chats for a clothing store, with the company's own rules for what agents should do.

Two jobs:

  • Triage: what does the customer want? Pick the broad intent (10 options) and the exact case (54 options).
  • Next action: given the chat so far, which of the 30 steps in the company playbook should the agent take next?

Three endpoints:

  • Jev, TypeSafe AI's hosted API (version 1.13).
  • ai_decide, Databricks' built-in decision function, called from SQL.
  • OpenAI Decisions, OpenAI's decision endpoint (GPT-6 Luna).

Two ways of asking (zero shot vs few shot):

  • Criteria only: one set of questions written from the company rules, with a short explanation for every option. Every endpoint gets exactly the same questions.
  • + examples: the same questions, plus the five most similar past chats with their correct answers, picked from a pool of 500 labelled chats. Part 2 explains how they're picked, and whether fine-tuning a small model does better.

Every endpoint answered the same 300 test chats, which none of them had seen before. The code to rerun it all is on GitHub. I used paired significance tests throughout, so when I say one is behind, the gap is real and not noise.

What's inside each one?

Same kind of API, three quite different things underneath:

  What's inside
Jev A dedicated, closed decision model, trained for exactly this job
ai_decide Not stated by Databricks. It behaves almost exactly like their open OpenJev model, so probably that (more below)
OpenAI Decisions A general small LLM, GPT-6 Luna, constrained to answer only with your options (how it's described)

What's behind ai_decide?

ai_decide accepts the same requests as Jev's API, so I expected it to be Jev. To check, I sent the same 150 chats to ai_decide, Jev (both versions 1.13 and 1.14) and Databricks' hosted OpenJev model, a small open decision model, and counted how often each pair gave the same answer (the script):

Same answer on… Broad intent Exact case Return yes/no
Jev 1.13 vs Jev 1.14 (two versions of one model, for scale) 98% 93% 99%
ai_decide vs Jev 1.14 96% 81% 96%
ai_decide vs OpenJev 96% 89% 100%

ai_decide disagrees with Jev more than two versions of Jev disagree with each other, and it's closest to OpenJev, matching it on every yes/no answer with near-identical probabilities. Databricks' own docs back this up: ai_decide runs on Apache 2.0-licensed models served through Databricks, and Jev's weights are closed. So treat ai_decide as Databricks' OpenJev behind Jev's API, not as Jev itself. Databricks doesn't say which model it runs, so that's my conclusion from the test, not an official fact.

Accuracy

Triage: broad intent (10 options) Jev: 0.87 with questions only, 0.91 with examples Jev 0.87 → 0.91 OpenAI Decisions: 0.88 with questions only, 0.92 with examples OpenAI Decisions 0.88 → 0.92 ai_decide: 0.86 with questions only, 0.91 with examples ai_decide 0.86 → 0.91 Triage: exact case (54 options) Jev: 0.79 with questions only, 0.87 with examples Jev 0.79 → 0.87 OpenAI Decisions: 0.79 with questions only, 0.86 with examples OpenAI Decisions 0.79 → 0.86 ai_decide: 0.70 with questions only, 0.73 with examples ai_decide 0.70 → 0.73 Next action (30 options) Jev: 0.56 with questions only, 0.71 with examples Jev 0.56 → 0.71 OpenAI Decisions: 0.57 with questions only, 0.63 with examples OpenAI Decisions 0.57 → 0.63 ai_decide: 0.39 with questions only, 0.43 with examples ai_decide 0.39 → 0.43 0.25 0.50 0.75 1.00 Accuracy on 300 test chats. Solid: questions only. Lighter extension: the gain from adding five similar labelled chats to the prompt. Black: Jev. Green: OpenAI Decisions. Blue: ai_decide.
  • Easy calls are a tie. All three score about the same on broad intent.
  • On the fine-grained calls, ai_decide falls behind, and barely gains from examples.
  • Examples help Jev most. That makes Jev with examples the clear winner on next action (0.71 vs OpenAI's 0.63).

Speed and cost

  Jev ai_decide OpenAI Decisions
Price $0.042 per million input tokens, output free Databricks compute (DBUs) $0.10 per million input tokens, output free
Per 1,000 calls $0.06–0.10 ($0.09–0.15 with examples) about $3 one call at a time; at most about $0.55 as one batch query (mostly start-up cost, so bigger batches are cheaper per call) $0.11–0.20 ($0.17–0.30 with examples)
Speed about 230 ms per call over the internet 300 chats in 19 s as one batch query about 300 ms per call over the internet
Your data Sent to TypeSafe AI (no training on it; zero retention for enterprise) Stays in your Databricks workspace Sent to OpenAI

 

Which to use

Use… When
Jev You want the most accurate hosted option, especially for fine-grained choices, and a hosted API is fine
ai_decide Your data is already in Databricks, the choices are broad, and you can run it as batch SQL. Test it on your fine-grained questions first
OpenAI Decisions You're already on OpenAI. It matches plain Jev for about 1.8× the price, but gains less from examples

Have a few hundred labelled examples? Adding the most similar ones to each prompt is the biggest single win for Jev, and in part 2 a fine-tuned 2B model catches up with it.

Caveats

  • One role-played dataset. Some labels are noisy, nothing reaches 100%, and your own data will differ. Treat this as a template for testing, not a verdict.
  • Any tuning bias favours Jev. I checked the questions against Jev's mistakes on separate dev chats, not the others'.
  • Speed isn't like-for-like. Jev and OpenAI were called over the internet from the UK, ai_decide through Databricks.
  • Connection errors. Some ai_decide calls hit a temporary Databricks network error and were re-run, so every chat has exactly one answer.

The code, the full results and every paired test are on GitHub: decision-model-bench (see RESULTS.md).

We cover all the latest AI updates in detail on our YouTube channel, so you can easily find out more information or know where to put your focus. Subscribe here. 

References

Chen, D., Chen, H., Yang, Y., Lin, A. and Yu, Z. (2021) 'Action-Based Conversations Dataset: A corpus for building more in-depth task-oriented dialogue systems', Proceedings of NAACL 2021, pp. 3002–3017. Available at: https://aclanthology.org/2021.naacl-main.239
